children.name: Serinus flavicola
children.description: A bright yellow-bellied species from East African savannas.

children.name: Serinus thibetanus
children.description: The Tibetan serin (Spinus thibetanus) or Tibetan siskin is a true finch species (family Fringillidae).

children.name: Serinus estherae
children.description: The Indonesian serin (Chrysocorythus estherae) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Crithagra
children.description: African seedeaters and canaries of savanna, scrub, and woodland.

children.name: Crithagra mozambica
children.description: The yellow-fronted canary (Crithagra mozambica) is a small passerine bird in the finch family..

children.name: Crithagra flaviventris
children.description: The yellow canary (Crithagra flaviventris) is a small passerine bird in the true finch family.

children.name: Crithagra sulphurata
children.description: The brimstone canary or bully canary (Crithagra sulphurata) is a small passerine bird in the finch family.

children.name: Crithagra leucopterus
children.description: A small, streaky seedeater of rocky slopes, open scrub, and highland grassland in equatorial Africa, notable for its bold white wing patches that flash conspicuously in flight. Often encountered in small flocks feeding on grass seeds and weed seeds in disturbed areas.

children.name: Crithagra striolatus
children.description: A heavily streaked and extremely common seedeater of highland scrub, gardens, and forest edges from Ethiopia to South Africa. One of the most abundant and vocal seedeaters in East African highland towns and roadsides, its song a persistent jangle from roadside shrubs.

children.name: Crithagra citrinipectus
children.description: The lemon-breasted canary (Crithagra citrinipectus), also known as the lemon-breasted seedeater, is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra alario
children.description: The black-headed canary (Serinus alario) is a species of finch found in Lesotho, Namibia and South Africa..

children.name: Crithagra albogularis
children.description: The white-throated canary (Crithagra albogularis) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra scotops
children.description: The forest canary (Crithagra scotops) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Crithagra atrogularis
children.description: The black-throated canary (Crithagra atrogularis), also known as the black-throated seedeater, is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra reichelarum
children.description: A West African canary; named after the ornithologist Anton Reichenow.

children.name: Crithagra gularis
children.description: The streaky-headed seedeater or streaky-headed canary (Crithagra gularis) is a small passerine bird in the finch family..

children.name: Crithagra reichenowi
children.description: Reichenow's seedeater (Crithagra reichenowi) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra mennelli
children.description: The black-eared seedeater or blackeared canary (Crithagra mennelli) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra strigosus
children.description: A heavily streaked brown canary of South African fynbos and karoo shrublands.

children.name: Crithagra citrinelloides
children.description: The African citril (Crithagra citrinelloides), also known as the Abyssinian citril, is a species of finch.

children.name: Crithagra hyposticta
children.description: The southern citril (Crithagra hyposticta or Serinus hyposticus) is a species of finch in the Fringillidae family.

children.name: Crithagra dorsostriata
children.description: The white-bellied canary (Crithagra dorsostriata) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra burtoni
children.description: The thick-billed seedeater (Crithagra burtoni) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra melanochroa
children.description: The Kipengere seedeater (Crithagra melanochroa), also known as the Tanzania seedeater, is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Crithagra tristriata
children.description: The brown-rumped seedeater (Crithagra tristriata) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra xanthopygia
children.description: The yellow-rumped seedeater, yellow-rumped serin or Abyssinian yellow-rumped seedeater (Crithagra xanthopygia) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra capistrata
children.description: The black-faced canary (Crithagra capistrata) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra whytii
children.description: The yellow-browed seedeater (Crithagra whytii) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra ankoberensis
children.description: The Ankober serin (Crithagra ankoberensis) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Crithagra flavigula
children.description: The yellow-throated seedeater (Crithagra flavigula) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra menachensis
children.description: The Yemen serin (Crithagra menachensis) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Crithagra xantholaema
children.description: Salvadori's seedeater or Salvadori's serin (Crithagra xantholaema) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra rufobrunnea
children.description: The Príncipe seedeater (Crithagra rufobrunnea) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Crithagra totta
children.description: The Cape siskin (Crithagra totta) is a small passerine bird in the finch family.

children.name: Haemorhous
children.description: New World rosefinches with red-washed males, common in North American habitats.

children.name: Haemorhous mexicanus
children.description: The house finch (Haemorhous mexicanus) is a North American bird in the finch family.

children.name: Haemorhous purpureus
children.description: The purple finch is a bird in the finch family, Fringillidae. It breeds in the northern United States, southern Canada, and the west coast of North America.

children.name: Haemorhous cassinii
children.description: Cassin's finch (Haemorhous cassinii) is a bird in the finch family, Fringillidae..

children.name: Haemorhous aneus
children.description: A colourful finch of western Mexican forests; the male is bright yellow with black wings.

children.name: Carpodacus
children.description: Old World rosefinches of mountains and northern forests, the males richly red.

children.name: Carpodacus erythrinus
children.description: The common rosefinch or scarlet rosefinch is the most widespread and common rosefinch of Asia and Europe.

children.name: Carpodacus rubicilla
children.description: thumb|Male in Hanle, Ladakh, India The great rosefinch (Carpodacus rubicilla) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Carpodacus pulcherrimus
children.description: The Himalayan beautiful rosefinch (Carpodacus pulcherrimus) is a true finch species (family Fringillidae)..

children.name: Carpodacus rhodochrous
children.description: A subtly beautiful rosefinch of Himalayan rhododendron scrub and conifer forests from Pakistan to Nepal, the male deep pink with a prominent pale supercilium. Inhabits dense montane forest between 2,500 and 4,000 m, descending to lower altitudes in severe winters.

children.name: Carpodacus roseus
children.description: Pallas's rosefinch (Carpodacus roseus) is a species of bird in the finch family Fringillidae..

children.name: Carpodacus synoicus
children.description: The Sinai rosefinch (Carpodacus synoicus) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Carpodacus puniceus
children.description: The red-fronted rosefinch (Carpodacus Puniceus) is a species of rosefinch in the finch family Fringillidae..

children.name: Carpodacus nipalensis
children.description: The dark-breasted rosefinch (Procarduelis nipalensis) is a species of true finch in the monotypic genus Procarduelis..

children.name: Carpodacus thura
children.description: The Himalayan white-browed rosefinch (Carpodacus thura) is a true finch species (family Fringillidae)..

children.name: Carpodacus edwardsii
children.description: The dark-rumped rosefinch (Carpodacus edwardsii) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Carpodacus waltoni
children.description: The pink-rumped rosefinch (Carpodacus waltoni) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Carpodacus verreauxii
children.description: Sharpe's rosefinch (Carpodacus verreauxii) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Carpodacus rubicinoides
children.description: A rosefinch of the Tibetan plateau with heavy streaking on the underparts.

children.name: Carpodacus trifasciatus
children.description: The three-banded rosefinch (Carpodacus trifasciatus) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Carpodacus rodopeplus
children.description: The spot-winged rosefinch (Carpodacus rodopeplus), also known as the spotted rosefinch, is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Carpodacus vernayi
children.description: A rosefinch of the northern Myanmar mountains, named after the naturalist Arthur Vernay.

children.name: Carpodacus stoliczkae
children.description: The pale rosefinch (Carpodacus stoliczkae) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Carpodacus vinaceus
children.description: The vinaceous rosefinch (Carpodacus vinaceus) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Carpodacus formosanus
children.description: The Taiwan rosefinch (Carpodacus formosanus) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Carpodacus davidianus
children.description: The Chinese beautiful rosefinch (Carpodacus davidianus) is a true finch species (family Fringillidae)..

children.name: Carpodacus severtzovi
children.description: The spotted great rosefinch or spotted rosefinch (Carpodacus rubicilla severtzovi) is a finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Pinicola
children.description: A single large, plump boreal finch of northern conifer forests worldwide.

children.name: Pinicola enucleator
children.description: The pine grosbeak is a large member of the true finch family, Fringillidae. It is the only species in the genus Pinicola. It is found in coniferous woods across Alaska, the western mountains of the United States, Canada, and in subarctic Fennoscandia and across the Palearctic to Siberia.

children.name: Leucosticte
children.description: Rosy finches — hardy montane finches of high-altitude snowfields, glaciers, and rocky alpine tundra in Asia and North America. They are among the few birds that spend the entire year above the treeline, foraging at the snow's edge for windblown seeds and invertebrates. Males develop a variable pink or rosy wash on the wings and rump.

children.name: Leucosticte tephrocotis
children.description: The gray-crowned rosy finch or gray-crowned rosy-finch (Leucosticte tephrocotis) is a species of passerine bird in the family Fringillidae native to Alaska, western Canada, and the north-western United States..

children.name: Leucosticte atrata
children.description: The black rosy finch or black rosy-finch (Leucosticte atrata) is a species of passerine bird in the family Fringillidae native to alpine areas above treeline, of the western United States.

children.name: Leucosticte australis
children.description: The brown-capped rosy finch (Leucosticte australis) is a medium-sized finch endemic to North America in the middle of the Rocky Mountains..

children.name: Leucosticte arctoa
children.description: The Asian rosy finch or Asian rosy-finch (Leucosticte arctoa) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Leucosticte brandti
children.description: Brandt's mountain finch (Leucosticte brandti), also known as the black-headed mountain-finch, is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Leucosticte nemoricola
children.description: The plain mountain finch (Leucosticte nemoricola) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Leucosticte sillemi
children.description: Sillem's rosefinch (Carpodacus sillemi), also known as Sillem's mountain finch or tawny-headed mountain finch is a species of rosefinch in the finch family..

children.name: Mycerobas
children.description: Allied grosbeaks — large, heavy-billed finches of Himalayan and Central Asian montane forests. The males are boldly patterned in black and yellow or red, and the massive bill is adapted for crushing large seeds and hard fruit stones. The genus is restricted to the montane forest zone of Asia from the western Himalayas east to China.

children.name: Mycerobas carnipes
children.description: The white-winged grosbeak (Mycerobas carnipes) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Mycerobas affinis
children.description: The collared grosbeak (Mycerobas affinis) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Mycerobas melanozanthos
children.description: The spot-winged grosbeak (Mycerobas melanozanthos) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae, found in middle to higher elevations..

children.name: Mycerobas icterioides
children.description: The black-and-yellow grosbeak (Mycerobas icterioides) is a species of finch native to the northern parts of the Indian subcontinent, primarily the lower and middle Himalayas..

children.name: Eophona
children.description: Japanese and Chinese grosbeaks — large, stocky finches of East Asian broadleaf and mixed forests with massive orange-yellow bills. They are powerful seed and cherry-stone crackers, the bill providing enough force to open hard fruit kernels unavailable to smaller finches. Both species have a black head and pale grey body, making them among the most striking finches in Asia.

children.name: Eophona migratoria
children.description: The Chinese grosbeak, yellow-billed grosbeak, or black-tailed hawfinch (Eophona migratoria) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Eophona personata
children.description: The Japanese grosbeak (Eophona personata) or Ikaru is a finch native to the East Palearctic.

children.name: Hesperiphona
children.description: New World grosbeaks of North and Central American conifer forests, closely related to the Old World grosbeaks. The males are dramatically patterned in yellow and black with white wing patches. These are irruptive birds, appearing in large numbers well outside their core range in years of food scarcity.

children.name: Hesperiphona vespertina
children.description: The evening grosbeak (Hesperiphona vespertina) is a passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae found in North America.

children.name: Hesperiphona abeillei
children.description: The hooded grosbeak or Albiellé's grosbeak is a passerine bird in the family Fringillidae, the finches and euphonias. It is found in Guatemala, El Salvador, and Mexico.

children.name: Bucanetes
children.description: Trumpeter and Mongolian finches — small, sandy-coloured desert finches of arid and semi-arid regions from the Canary Islands and North Africa across the Middle East to Central Asia. Males have a pink or rosy wash on the plumage and bill. Their distinctive calls, often described as nasal or trumpet-like, carry well across open desert terrain.

children.name: Bucanetes githagineus
children.description: thumb|Bucanetes githagineus amantum [[MHNT]].

children.name: Bucanetes mongolicus
children.description: The Mongolian finch (Bucanetes mongolicus), also known as the Mongolian trumpeter finch, is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae.

children.name: Drepanis
children.description: Hawaiian mamos and the Iiwi — iconic Hawaiian honeycreepers with long, curved bills evolved for accessing the nectar of native lobeliad flowers. The Iiwi is one of the most recognisable birds in the Hawaiian archipelago; its brilliant scarlet plumage and sickle-shaped bill make it unmistakable. Hawaiian honeycreepers are now placed within Fringillidae based on genomic data.

children.name: Drepanis coccinea
children.description: The ʻiʻiwi (pronounced , ee-EE-wee or , ee-EE-vee) or scarlet honeycreeper (Drepanis coccinea) is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper..

children.name: Drepanis pacifica
children.description: The Hawaii mamo (Drepanis pacifica) is an extinct species of Hawaiian honeycreeper.

children.name: Drepanis funerea
children.description: The black mamo (Drepanis funerea), also known as the hoa, is an extinct species of Hawaiian honeycreeper once endemic to the island of Molokai; there is also subfossil evidence of it having lived on Maui.

children.name: Himatione
children.description: The Apapane — a crimson Hawaiian honeycreeper that is among the most abundant of all surviving Hawaiian forest birds. Unlike many of its relatives, the Apapane has maintained larger populations in part due to its ability to exploit a wider range of ohia habitat.

children.name: Himatione sanguinea
children.description: The ʻapapane ( AH-pah-PAH-nay;) (Himatione sanguinea) is a small, crimson species of Hawaiian honeycreeper endemic to the Hawaiian Islands..

children.name: Himatione fraithii
children.description: The Laysan honeycreeper (Himatione fraithii), also known as the Laysan apapane or Laysan honeyeater, is an extinct species of finch that was endemic to the island of Laysan in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands.

children.name: Loxops
children.description: Small Hawaiian honeycreepers with a unique bill shape where the tips cross slightly.

children.name: Loxops coccineus
children.description: The Hawaiʻi ʻākepa (Loxops coccineus) is an endangered ʻākepa native to Hawaiʻi in the Hawaiian Islands..

children.name: Loxops caeruleirostris
children.description: The akekeʻe or Kauaʻi ʻākepa is a bird species in the family Fringillidae, where it is placed in the Hawaiian honeycreeper genus Loxops. It is endemic to the island of Kauaʻi where it is found in small numbers in higher elevations. Because of their similar size, shape, and unusual bill, the akekeʻe and the Hawaiʻi ʻākepa were for some time classified as a single species.

children.name: Loxops mana
children.description: The Hawaiʻi creeper, Hawaii creeper or alawī (Loxops mana) is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper endemic to the Big Island of Hawaiʻi..

children.name: Loxops ochraceus
children.description: The Maui ʻākepa (Loxops ochraceus) is an extinct species of ʻākepa that was endemic to Maui in the Hawaiian Islands..

children.name: Hemignathus
children.description: Hawaiian honeycreepers with extremely long curved bills for extracting nectar from lobelioid flowers.

children.name: Hemignathus wilsoni
children.description: The ʻakiapōlāʻau, also known as the Hawaiian woodpecker, is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper that is endemic to the island of Hawaii. Its natural habitats are dry and montane moist forests, and it is the only bird species on the island to occupy the woodpecker niche. The bird is 5.5 inches (14 cm) in length, and has an unusually curved beak-(a specialist species).

children.name: Hemignathus munroi
children.description: The ʻakiapōlāʻau (ah-kee-ah-POH-lah-ow), also known as the Hawaiian woodpecker, is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper that is endemic to the island of Hawaii..

children.name: Hemignathus lucidus
children.description: The Oʻahu nukupuʻu (Hemignathus lucidus) is an extinct species of  nukupuʻu, a type of Hawaiian honeycreeper native to Oahu, which was similar to its cousins from the Islands of Kauaʻi and Maui..

children.name: Hemignathus ellisianus
children.description: The Oʻahu ʻakialoa (Akialoa ellisiana)  is an extinct species of Hawaiian honeycreeper in the subfamily Carduelinae of the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Spiza
children.description: A grassland bird of the central USA; the sole member of its genus; winters in large flocks in South America.

children.name: Spiza americana
children.description: The dickcissel (Spiza americana) is a small seed-eating migratory bird in the family Cardinalidae..

children.name: Telespiza
children.description: Laysan and Nihoa finches of remote northwestern Hawaiian atolls, evolved as omnivorous survivors on tiny coral islands with limited resources.

children.name: Telespiza cantans
children.description: The Laysan finch (Telespiza cantans), sometimes referred to by its Hawaiian name, ʻekupuʻu, is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper, that is endemic to the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands.

children.name: Telespiza ultima
children.description: The Nīhoa finch (Telespiza ultima) is one of the two endemic bird species of the tiny Hawaiian island of Nīhoa, the other being the Nīhoa millerbird..

children.name: Palmeria
children.description: The Akohekohe — one of the most spectacular Hawaiian honeycreepers, with an extraordinary crest and vivid orange-red plumage patches.

children.name: Palmeria dolei
children.description: The ʻākohekohe, or crested honeycreeper, is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper. It is endemic to the island of Maui in Hawaiʻi. The ʻākohekohe is susceptible to mosquito‐transmitted avian malaria and only breeds in high‐elevation wet forests.

children.name: Pseudonestor
children.description: The Maui Parrotbill — a critically endangered Hawaiian honeycreeper with a massively powerful, parrot-like bill for tearing apart wood to find beetle larvae.

children.name: Pseudonestor xanthophrys
children.description: The kiwikiu or Maui parrotbill (Pseudonestor xanthophrys) is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper endemic to the island of Maui in Hawaii.

children.name: Melamprosops
children.description: The Poo-uli — discovered in 1973, extinct by 2004. It represented a unique evolutionary lineage with no close relatives among known Hawaiian birds.

children.name: Melamprosops phaeosoma
children.description: The poʻo-uli (Melamprosops phaeosoma)  or  Hawaiian black-faced honeycreeper is an extinct species of passerine bird that was endemic to the island of Maui in Hawaiʻi..

children.name: Oreomystis
children.description: The Akikiki — a tiny bark-creeping honeycreeper confined to Kauai's native forest, now one of the most critically endangered birds in the world.

children.name: Oreomystis bairdi
children.description: The ʻakikiki (pronounced ) (Oreomystis bairdi), also called the Kauaʻi creeper, is a critically endangered Hawaiian honeycreeper endemic to Kauaʻi, Hawaiʻi..

children.name: Paroreomyza
children.description: Hawaiian creepers — small bark-foraging honeycreepers, several species of which are now extinct due to introduced rats and avian disease.

children.name: Paroreomyza maculata
children.description: The Oʻahu ʻalauahio (Paroreomyza maculata), also known as the Oʻahu creeper, is a small finch-like Hawaiian honeycreeper that is endemic to the Hawaiian island of Oahu..

children.name: Paroreomyza flammea
children.description: The kākāwahie or Molokaʻi creeper (Paroreomyza flammea) is an extinct species of Hawaiian honeycreeper..

children.name: Magumma
children.description: The Anianiau — the smallest Hawaiian honeycreeper and one of the few with a relatively stable population, confined to Kauai's native forest.

children.name: Magumma parva
children.description: The ʻanianiau (pronounced ) (Magumma parva) is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper that is endemic to upper elevation forests on the island of Kauai..

children.name: Chloridops
children.description: The Kona Grosbeak — an extinct Hawaiian honeycreeper with an enormously massive bill for crushing the hard seeds of the naio tree, last seen in 1894.

children.name: Chloridops kona
children.description: The Kona grosbeak (Chloridops kona) is an extinct species of Hawaiian honeycreeper.

children.name: Rhodacanthis
children.description: Koa finches — extinct Hawaiian honeycreepers with large bills adapted for crushing native koa pods, eliminated by introduced rats and forest clearance in the 19th century.

children.name: Rhodacanthis flaviceps
children.description: The lesser koa finch (Rhodacanthis flaviceps) is an extinct species of Hawaiian honeycreeper in the subfamily Carduelinae of the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Rhodacanthis palmeri
children.description: The greater koa finch (Rhodacanthis palmeri) is an extinct species of Hawaiian honeycreeper in the subfamily Carduelinae of the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Loxioides
children.description: The Palila — a critically endangered Hawaiian honeycreeper entirely dependent on the mamane tree, and the subject of landmark environmental law cases in the USA.

children.name: Loxioides bailleui
children.description: The palila (Loxioides bailleui) is a critically endangered finch-billed species of Hawaiian honeycreeper..

children.name: Chlorodrepanis
children.description: Hawaiian amakihis — adaptable honeycreepers showing documented genetic resistance to avian malaria, allowing recolonisation of lower elevations than other honeycreepers can survive.

children.name: Chlorodrepanis virens
children.description: The Hawaiʻi ʻamakihi (Chlorodrepanis virens), also known as the common ʻamakihi, is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper..

children.name: Chlorodrepanis flava
children.description: The Oʻahu ʻamakihi (Chlorodrepanis flava) is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Chlorodrepanis stejnegeri
children.description: The Kauaʻi ʻamakihi (Chlorodrepanis stejnegeri) is a species of Hawaiian honeycreepers endemic to Kauaʻi in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Rhodospiza
children.description: The Desert Finch — a distinctive pale finch of Central Asian and Middle Eastern arid zones; the sole member of its genus.

children.name: Rhodospiza obsoleta
children.description: thumb|250px|Rhodospiza obsoleta The desert finch (Rhodospiza obsoleta), sometimes called Lichtenstein's desert finch, is a large brown true finch found in southern Eurasia.

children.name: Callacanthis
children.description: The Spectacled Finch — a striking high-altitude finch of Himalayan conifer forests, the male bearing bold red supercilia and red-spotted wings; the sole member of its genus.

children.name: Callacanthis burtoni
children.description: The spectacled finch (Callacanthis burtoni) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae.

children.name: Pyrrhoplectes
children.description: The Gold-naped Finch — a jewel-like finch of dense Himalayan bamboo and rhododendron undergrowth, the male bearing a stunning gold-orange nape against jet-black plumage.

children.name: Pyrrhoplectes epauletta
children.description: The golden-naped finch (Pyrrhoplectes epauletta) is a species of finch in the family Fringillidae..

children.name: Haematospiza
children.description: The Scarlet Finch — a vivid scarlet finch of Himalayan and Southeast Asian montane forests, the brilliantly coloured male one of the most eye-catching birds in the region.

children.name: Haematospiza sipahi
children.description: The scarlet finch (Carpodacus sipahi) is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae.

children.name: Uragus
children.description: The Long-tailed Rosefinch — a delicate, pale pink finch of willow and birch scrub along rivers across Siberia and East Asia, with a distinctive long, forked tail.

children.name: Uragus sibiricus

children.name: Oenanthe deserti

It is a migratory insectivorous species, 14.5 to 15 cm in length. Both western and eastern forms of the desert wheatear are rare vagrants to western Europe.

children.name: Oenanthe monacha

It is the most widespread member of the wheatear genus Oenanthe in Europe and North and Central Asia. The northern wheatear is a migratory insectivorous species breeding in open stony country in Europe and east across the Palearctic with footholds in northeastern Canada and Greenland as well as in northwestern Canada and Alaska.

children.name: Oenanthe pleschanka

This migratory central Asiatic wheatear occurs from the extreme southeast of Europe to China, and has been found wintering in India and northeastern Africa. It is a very rare vagrant to western Europe.

children.name: Motacilla
children.description: Wagtails — slender, long-tailed passerines named for their incessant tail-pumping, which serves as a signal of alertness to potential predators. The white wagtail (sädesärla) is one of Sweden's most familiar and beloved birds, nesting on buildings, farms, jetties, and bridges across the country. It is among the first migratory birds to return in spring — its appearance is greeted as a sure sign that winter is ending. Wagtails walk with an elegant, deliberate gait, chasing insects on short sprints along the ground. They are strongly associated with human habitation in Sweden, and the sight and sound of a sädesärla bobbing on a roof is embedded in Swedish cultural memory.

children.name: Motacilla alba
children.description: The white wagtail is a small passerine bird in the family Motacillidae, which also includes pipits and longclaws. The species breeds in the Palearctic zone in most of Europe and Asia and parts of North Africa; it also has a toehold in western Alaska as a scarce breeder. It is resident in the mildest parts of its range, but otherwise migrates to Africa.

children.name: Motacilla flava
children.description: The western yellow wagtail is a small passerine bird in the wagtail family Motacillidae, which also includes the pipits and longclaws. This species breeds in much of temperate Europe and Asia. Most populations are migratory, moving south to tropical Africa and southern Asia for the winter; the small population breeding in Egypt is however resident there.

children.name: Motacilla cinerea
children.description: The grey wagtail is a member of the wagtail family, Motacillidae, measuring around 18–19 cm overall length. The species looks somewhat similar to the yellow wagtail but has the yellow on its underside restricted to the throat and vent. Breeding males have a black throat.

children.name: Motacilla capensis
children.description: The Cape wagtail (Motacilla capensis), also known as Wells's wagtail, is a small insectivorous bird which is widespread in southern Africa.

children.name: Motacilla citreola
children.description: The citrine wagtail is a small songbird in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Motacilla clara
children.description: The mountain wagtail (Motacilla clara), also known as the long-tailed wagtail or grey-backed wagtail, is a species of wagtail of the family Motacillidae from sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Motacilla flaviventris
children.description: The Madagascar wagtail (Motacilla flaviventris) is a species of wagtail in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Motacilla grandis
children.description: The Japanese wagtail (Motacilla grandis) is a species of bird in the pipit and wagtail family Motacillidae.

children.name: Motacilla lugens
children.description: The white wagtail (Motacilla alba) is a small passerine bird in the family Motacillidae, which also includes pipits and longclaws.

children.name: Motacilla samveasnae
children.description: The Mekong wagtail (Motacilla samveasnae) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Dendronanthus
children.description: Forest Wagtail — a monotypic genus comprising a single highly distinctive species that differs from all other wagtails in its arboreal habits, nesting in trees and foraging on forest floors. It wags its tail sideways rather than up-and-down, a unique behaviour among the family.

children.name: Dendronanthus indicus
children.description: The forest wagtail (Dendronanthus indicus) is a medium-sized passerine bird in the wagtail family Motacillidae.

children.name: Tmetothylacus
children.description: Golden Pipit — a monotypic genus containing one of the most spectacular members of the family, the brilliant golden yellow Golden Pipit of East African savannas. Unlike most pipits it shows sexual dichromatism, with males dazzlingly yellow and black and females more streaked olive-brown.

children.name: Tmetothylacus tenellus
children.description: The golden pipit (Tmetothylacus tenellus) is a distinctive pipit of dry country grassland, savanna and shrubland in eastern Africa.

children.name: Macronyx
children.description: Longclaws — large, robust African pipits characterised by a broad yellow, orange, or pink throat patch bordered by a bold black necklace, and exceptionally long hind claws adapted for walking through tall grass. They occupy open grasslands, marshes, and mountain meadows across sub-Saharan Africa and superficially resemble North American meadowlarks through convergent evolution.

children.name: Macronyx aurantiigula
children.description: thumb|Pangani Longclaw The Pangani longclaw (Macronyx aurantiigula) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae, which includes the pipits and wagtails.

children.name: Macronyx capensis
children.description: The Cape longclaw or orange-throated longclaw (Macronyx capensis) is a passerine bird in the family Motacillidae, which comprises the longclaws, pipits and wagtails.

children.name: Macronyx flavicollis
children.description: The Abyssinian longclaw (Macronyx flavicollis) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Anthus
children.description: Pipits — streaky brown passerines of open habitats, the sparrows of the moor and meadow. Pipits can be difficult to identify by plumage but their songs and calls are distinctive — the meadow pipit gives a thin, insistent 'seep' in flight. The tree pipit (trädpiplärka) sings a wonderful descending song, delivered in a parachuting display flight from a tree perch — one of the joyful sounds of Swedish woodland clearings in spring. Meadow pipits are extraordinarily numerous across Scandinavian moorland and bogland and are the primary host of the common cuckoo in many areas. Pipits walk (rather than hop) and wag their tails gently, unlike the more vigorous pumping of true wagtails.

children.name: Anthus pratensis
children.description: The meadow pipit is a small passerine bird that breeds throughout much of the Palearctic, from south-eastern Greenland and Iceland east to just east of the Ural Mountains in Russia, and south to central France and Romania; an isolated population also occurs in the Caucasus Mountains. It is migratory over most of its range, wintering in southern Europe, North Africa, and south-western Asia, but is resident year-round in western Europe, although even here many birds move to the coast or lowlands in winter.

children.name: Anthus trivialis
children.description: The tree pipit is a small passerine bird that breeds throughout most of Europe and the Palearctic as far east as the East Siberian Mountains. It is a long-distance migrant, migrating in winter to Africa and southern Asia. The scientific name is from Latin: anthus is the name of a small bird of grasslands, and the specific  trivialis means "common".

children.name: Anthus cervinus
children.description: The red-throated pipit is a small passerine bird, which breeds in the far north of Europe and the Palearctic, with a foothold in northern Alaska. It is a long-distance migrant, wintering to Africa and South-East Asia and western Alaska in North America. It is vagrant to Western Europe.

children.name: Anthus bogotensis
children.description: The paramo pipit (Anthus bogotensis) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae, the wagtails and pipits.

children.name: Anthus caffer
children.description: The bushveld pipit (Anthus caffer), also known as bush pipit or little pipit, is a species of bird in the pipit and wagtail family Motacillidae.

children.name: Anthus campestris
children.description: The tawny pipit is a medium-large passerine bird which breeds in much of the central Palearctic from northwest Africa and Portugal to Central Siberia and on to Inner Mongolia. It is a migrant moving in winter to tropical Africa and the Indian subcontinent.

children.name: Anthus chacoensis
children.description: The Pampas pipit (Anthus chacoensis) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae, the wagtails and pipits.

children.name: Anthus cinnamomeus
children.description: The African pipit (Anthus cinnamomeus) is a fairly small passerine bird belonging to the pipit genus Anthus in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Anthus correndera
children.description: The correndera pipit (Anthus correndera) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae, the wagtails and pipits.

children.name: Anthus godlewskii
children.description: Blyth's pipit is a medium-sized passerine bird which breeds in Mongolia and neighbouring areas of China, Tibet and India. It is a long distance migrant moving to open lowlands in Southern Asia. It is a very rare vagrant to western Europe.

children.name: Anthus gustavi
children.description: The Pechora pipit (Anthus gustavi) is a small passerine bird which breeds in the East Palearctic tundra and densely vegetated areas near river banks ranges from the Pechora River to the Chukchi Peninsula.

children.name: Anthus gutturalis
children.description: The alpine pipit (Anthus gutturalis) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Anthus hoeschi
children.description: The mountain pipit (Anthus hoeschi) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Anthus lineiventris
children.description: The striped pipit (Anthus lineiventris) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae, which is native to Africa southwards of the equator.

children.name: Anthus lutescens
children.description: The yellowish pipit (Anthus chii) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae, the wagtails and pipits.

children.name: Anthus melindae
children.description: The Malindi pipit (Anthus melindae) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Anthus nattereri
children.description: The ochre-breasted pipit is a Vulnerable species of bird in the family Motacillidae, the wagtails and pipits. It is found in Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay.

children.name: Anthus nilghiriensis
children.description: The Nilgiri pipit (Anthus nilghiriensis) is a distinctive species of pipit that is endemic to the high altitude hills of southern India.

children.name: Anthus nitidulus
children.description: A lightly built, neatly streaked pipit of open grasslands, scrubby clearings, and roadsides across the Philippine Islands and Sulawesi. It is one of the few pipits in the Philippines and is the common open-country pipit of lowland areas. Its relatively fine bill and clean face pattern with a prominent pale supercilium distinguish it from vagrants.

children.name: Anthus nyassae
children.description: The wood pipit or woodland pipit (Anthus nyassae) is a small passerine bird belonging to the pipit genus Anthus in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Anthus peruvianus
children.description: The Peruvian pipit (Anthus peruvianus) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae, the wagtails and pipits.

children.name: Anthus petrosus
children.description: The European rock pipit (Anthus petrosus), or simply rock pipit, is a species of small passerine bird that breeds in western Europe on rocky coasts.

children.name: Anthus richardi
children.description: Richard's pipit is a medium-sized passerine bird which breeds in open grasslands in the East Palearctic. It is a long-distance migrant moving to open lowlands in the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. It is a rare but regular vagrant to western Europe.

children.name: Anthus roseatus
children.description: The Rosy pipit (Anthus roseatus) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Anthus rubescens
children.description: The American pipit (Anthus rubescens), formerly known as the buff-bellied pipit, is a small songbird native to North America.

children.name: Anthus rufulus
children.description: The paddyfield pipit or Oriental pipit (Anthus rufulus) is a small passerine bird in the pipit and wagtail family.

children.name: Anthus sokokensis
children.description: The Sokoke pipit (Anthus sokokensis) is a species of bird in the family Motacillidae.

children.name: Anthus spinoletta
children.description: The water pipit (Anthus spinoletta) is a small passerine bird which breeds in the mountains of Southern Europe and the Palearctic eastwards to China.

children.name: Anthus vaalensis
children.description: The buffy pipit (Anthus vaalensis) is a species of bird in the Motacillidae family.

children.name: Hirundo
children.description: Barn swallows — the most familiar swallows on Earth and one of the most widespread birds in the world. The barn swallow (ladusvala) is a summer visitor of immense cultural significance in Sweden: its arrival in late April or early May is celebrated as a defining moment of the Nordic year. Swallows have lived alongside humans for millennia, nesting in barns, stables, and buildings and feeding on the insects attracted to livestock — a mutualistic relationship that has made them simultaneously dependent on and beloved by farming communities. Swallows are aerial masters, capable of sustained flight speeds exceeding 70 km/h and catching all their food on the wing. They are long-distance migrants, wintering in sub-Saharan Africa and covering up to 10,000 km each way.

children.name: Hirundo rustica
children.description: The barn swallow is the most widespread species of swallow in the world, occurring on all continents, with vagrants reported even in Antarctica. It is a distinctive passerine bird with blue upperparts and a long, deeply forked tail. In Anglophone Europe, it is just called the swallow; in northern Europe, it is the only member of family Hirundinidae called a "swallow" rather than a "martin".

children.name: Hirundo angolensis
children.description: The Angola swallow (Hirundo angolensis) is a species of swallow that is native to the Afrotropics.

children.name: Hirundo tahitica
children.description: The Tahiti swallow (Hirundo tahitica) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Hirundo neoxena
children.description: The welcome swallow (Hirundo neoxena) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae that is native to Australia and nearby islands.

children.name: Hirundo aethiopica
children.description: The Ethiopian swallow (Hirundo aethiopica) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Cecropis
children.description: Striated and rufous swallows — a genus of Old World swallows split from Hirundo, characterized by streaked or rufous underparts and often prominent rufous rumps. They are found across Africa and Asia, with one species extending to Europe and another resident in Australia. Several are associated with rocky gorges and cliffs, while others nest in buildings and under bridges.

children.name: Cecropis senegalensis
children.description: The mosque swallow (Cecropis senegalensis) is a large species of swallow.

children.name: Petrochelidon
children.description: Cliff swallows and allies — a genus of colonial swallows that build retort-shaped mud nests on cliff faces and man-made structures. The group spans North America, Africa, and Australia. The American cliff swallow is one of the most spectacular colonial birds in North America, with colonies sometimes numbering tens of thousands of nests under highway overpasses.

children.name: Petrochelidon pyrrhonota
children.description: The cliff swallow or American cliff swallow (Petrochelidon pyrrhonota) is a member of the passerine bird family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Petrochelidon fulva
children.description: The cave swallow (Petrochelidon fulva) is a medium-sized, squarish-tailed swallow belonging to the same genus as the more familiar and widespread cliff swallow of North America.

children.name: Petrochelidon nigricans
children.description: The tree martin (Petrochelidon nigricans) is a member of the swallow family of passerine birds.

children.name: Petrochelidon ariel
children.description: The fairy martin (Petrochelidon ariel) is a member of the swallow family of passerine birds which breeds in Australia.

children.name: Petrochelidon frontalis
children.description: A colonial cliff swallow of the Himalayan foothills and hills of South and Southeast Asia, building enclosed mud nests on rocky cliff faces and under bridges. It is closely related to the streak-throated swallow and was long treated as its subspecies. The species has a more restricted distribution in the foothills of Nepal, Bangladesh, and adjacent Myanmar.

children.name: Delichon
children.description: House martins — compact, blue-black and white swallows that build dome-shaped mud nests attached to cliff faces and — most famously — under the eaves of houses. The common house martin (hussvala) is a familiar summer visitor to Swedish towns and villages, and established colonies under roof eaves can be decades old. House martins collect mud for nest construction from puddles and stream banks, sometimes travelling considerable distances from their nesting site. They are more colonial than barn swallows, often building nests immediately adjacent to one another. Despite their name and intimate association with human buildings, relatively little is known about their winter quarters in sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Delichon urbicum
children.description: The western house martin, sometimes called the common house martin, northern house martin or, particularly in Europe, just house martin, is a migratory passerine bird of the swallow family which breeds in Europe, north Africa and west-central Asia; and winters in sub-Saharan Africa and southwestern Asia. It feeds on insects which are caught in flight, and it migrates to climates where flying insects are plentiful. It has a blue head and upperparts, white rump and pure white underparts, and is found in both open country and near human habitation.

children.name: Riparia
children.description: Sand martins — the smallest and brownest of Sweden's swallows, colonial nesters in sandy riverbanks, sand quarries, and sea cliffs. Each pair excavates a tunnel 30–90 cm deep in bare sand, ending in a nesting chamber — a feat of engineering for a bird weighing just 13 grams. Sand martin colonies can number thousands of pairs and create dramatic, buzzing spectacles when the birds return to their colony after feeding. They are among the earliest summer migrants to arrive in Sweden in spring, and their presence at a colony site can be assessed instantly by the dark rings of nest holes peppering the sand face.

children.name: Riparia riparia
children.description: The sand martin, also known as the collared sand martin or common sand martin, and in the Americas as the bank swallow, is a migratory passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae. It has a wide range in summer, embracing practically the whole Holarctic area, from Europe, across Asia to the Pacific Ocean, and throughout North America. It winters in eastern and southern Africa, southern Asia, and South America.

children.name: Riparia congica
children.description: The Congo martin or Congo sand martin (Riparia congica) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Riparia cincta
children.description: The banded martin or banded sand martin (Neophedina cincta) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae that is endemic to Africa.

children.name: Riparia diluta
children.description: The pale martin or pale sand martin (Riparia diluta) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Ptyonoprogne
children.description: Crag martins — robust, earth-coloured swallows of rocky mountains and gorges. The Eurasian crag martin nests on cliff faces and rocky outcrops, plastering a mud cup to vertical rock surfaces in locations completely inaccessible to terrestrial predators. They are resident year-round in southern Europe's mountain ranges, one of the few swallows that don't make long-distance migrations. In Sweden, crag martins are rare vagrants rather than breeding birds, occasionally seen along coastal cliffs in autumn. Their flight is more leisurely and gliding than other swallows, matching the thermal-soaring conditions of mountain environments.

children.name: Ptyonoprogne rupestris
children.description: The Eurasian crag martin or just crag martin (Ptyonoprogne rupestris) is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Pseudhirundo
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the grey-rumped swallow of sub-Saharan Africa. The grey-rumped swallow is an unusual African hirundine that was long associated with Riparia but differs in its grey rump and preference for forest edge habitats. It builds its nest in burrows in banks or old woodpecker holes in trees.

children.name: Psalidoprocne
children.description: Saw-wings — a genus of African swallows named for the serrated outer primary feathers of the males, a unique structural feature among birds. They inhabit forest, woodland, and edge habitats across sub-Saharan Africa. Saw-wings are often associated with forest streams and ravines, and their flight style is more fluttering and bat-like than that of open-country swallows.

children.name: Psalidoprocne holomelaena
children.description: A widespread, entirely black saw-wing found across east and southern Africa in montane forest and adjacent woodland. It is the most frequently observed saw-wing in much of eastern Africa. Both sexes are uniformly black, lacking the contrasting white head of some relatives.

children.name: Psalidoprocne obscura
children.description: thumb|Fanti saw-wing in [[Brufut forest, The Gambia]] The Fanti saw-wing (Psalidoprocne obscura), also known as the Fanti rough-winged swallow, is a small passerine bird in the swallow family.

children.name: Phedina
children.description: A small genus of African martins with streaked underparts, found in Madagascar and central Africa. They inhabit open country near water and forest clearings, and are among the less well-studied hirundines. The Mascarene martin is a migratory species that moves between breeding and wintering areas within the Indian Ocean region.

children.name: Phedina borbonica
children.description: The Mascarene martin or Mascarene swallow is a passerine bird in the swallow family that breeds in Madagascar and in the Mascarene Islands. The nominate subspecies occurs on Mauritius and Réunion and has never been found away from the Mascarene Islands, but the smaller Madagascan subspecies, P. madagascariensis, is migratory and has been recorded wintering in East Africa or wandering to other Indian Ocean islands.

children.name: Progne
children.description: Purple martins and their allies — the largest swallows in the Americas, with glossy blue-black plumage in males and more dusky or brown females. Progne martins are strongly associated with human-provided nest boxes and gourds in North America, where the purple martin has become almost entirely dependent on man-made nest structures east of the Rockies. South American species tend to inhabit open savanna and forest edge, often nesting in palm cavities.

children.name: Progne subis
children.description: The purple martin (Progne subis) is a passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Progne cryptoleuca
children.description: The Cuban martin (Progne cryptoleuca) is a large swallow endemic to Cuba.

children.name: Progne dominicensis
children.description: | range_map = Progne dominicensis map.svg.

children.name: Progne elegans
children.description: The southern martin (Progne elegans) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Progne murphyi
children.description: The Peruvian martin (Progne murphyi) is a Near Threatened species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Progne sinaloae
children.description: The Sinaloa martin (Progne sinaloae) is a Vulnerable species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Tachycineta
children.description: A New World genus of iridescent green, blue, or violet swallows, including the tree swallow — one of the most studied birds in the world due to its enthusiastic adoption of nest boxes. Tachycineta swallows range from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, with several island endemics in the Caribbean. Their tree swallow populations have served as a model for understanding the effects of climate change on avian breeding phenology.

children.name: Tachycineta bicolor
children.description: The tree swallow (Tachycineta bicolor) is a migratory bird of the family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Tachycineta cyaneoviridis
children.description: The Bahama swallow (Tachycineta cyaneoviridis) is an endangered swallow endemic to The Bahamas.

children.name: Tachycineta stolzmanni
children.description: The Tumbes swallow (Tachycineta stolzmanni) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Tachycineta meyeni
children.description: The Chilean swallow (Tachycineta leucopyga) is a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae.

children.name: Tachycineta euchrysea
children.description: The golden swallow (Tachycineta euchrysea) is a swallow endemic to the Caribbean island of Hispaniola (split between the Dominican Republic and Haiti) and was once native to Jamaica, but is now extirpated there.

children.name: Tachycineta albilinea
children.description: ]] The mangrove swallow (Tachycineta albilinea) is a passerine bird in the swallow family that breeds in coastal regions from Mexico through Central America to Panama.

children.name: Stelgidopteryx
children.description: Rough-winged swallows — a New World genus of two species named for the tiny hook-like serrations on the outer primary feathers of the males. They are dull brown swallows without the iridescent plumage of many relatives, but are widespread and common in a variety of open habitats throughout the Americas. They nest in burrows and crevices in earth banks, often using old kingfisher holes.

children.name: Stelgidopteryx serripennis
children.description: The northern rough-winged swallow (Stelgidopteryx serripennis) is a small, migratory swallow.

children.name: Stelgidopteryx ruficollis
children.description: The southern rough-winged swallow (Stelgidopteryx ruficollis) a species of bird in the family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.

children.name: Cheramoeca
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the white-backed swallow, one of Australia's most distinctively patterned hirundines. The genus is characterised by a unique combination of features including a deeply forked tail, white back, and pied plumage. The white-backed swallow occupies arid and semi-arid Australia, nesting in burrows it excavates in sandy soil.

children.name: Alopochelidon
children.description: A monotypic genus comprising the tawny-headed swallow of South America. The genus has sometimes been placed within Stelgidopteryx but morphological and molecular data support its recognition as a distinct genus. The tawny-headed swallow is a bird of open woodland and savanna in central South America.

children.name: Atticora
children.description: A genus of two elegant Amazonian swallows with distinctive banded or jet-black plumage. Atticora swallows are associated with major Amazonian rivers and their tributaries. They nest colonially in sandy riverbanks and are among the more distinctive hirundines of the Amazon basin.

children.name: Atticora andecola
children.description: A high-altitude swallow of the open Andean puna, found from Peru south to northwestern Argentina and Chile at elevations typically above 3,500 m. It is the least typical Atticora, with plain brown upperparts and pale underparts, and was formerly placed in its own genus Haplochelidon. The species nests in burrows in earthen banks and is locally migratory in the non-breeding season.

children.name: Neochelidon
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the white-thighed swallow of northern South America, sometimes placed in Atticora. It is a small, dark swallow of forest edge and open country in lowland Amazonia and adjacent areas, identified by its white thigh tufts visible in flight.

children.name: Pygochelidon
children.description: A genus of two Andean and southern South American swallows formerly placed in Notiochelidon. They are small, blue-black swallows of open Andean habitats and Patagonian grasslands, often nesting in towns and villages at high altitude.

children.name: Pygochelidon patagonica
children.description: A recently separated species, formerly treated as the migratory subspecies of the blue-and-white swallow, breeding in Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego. It is a long-distance austral migrant, wintering as far north as Bolivia and Brazil. The species inhabits open Patagonian steppe and grassland near water.

children.name: Orochelidon
children.description: Andean martins — a genus of two high-altitude swallows of the Andes formerly placed in Notiochelidon. They inhabit open Andean puna and grassland, often at elevations above 3,000 m. Both are dark swallows with pale underparts and are typical aerial feeders of the open Andean sky.

children.name: Pseudochelidon
children.description: River martins — a primitive genus of two highly distinctive swallows placed in their own subfamily, Pseudochelidoninae, owing to their aberrant morphology: they have large eyes, heavy bills, stout legs, and rounded wings unlike any other hirundine. The African river martin breeds on sandbars in the Congo River, while the white-eyed river martin was last confirmed on its Thai wintering grounds in the 1970s and may be extinct.

children.name: Phylloscopus
children.description: Leaf warblers — small, active, largely green or yellow-green warblers that glean insects from foliage with remarkable agility. The willow warbler is the single most numerous summer bird in Sweden, estimated at over 40 million breeding pairs across Scandinavia. Despite weighing just 9 grams, it completes an annual round trip of 10,000–14,000 km to sub-Saharan Africa and back. The genus spans the entire Palearctic from Atlantic Europe to the Pacific, with diversity peaking in the Himalayas and China.

children.name: Phylloscopus trochilus
children.description: The willow warbler is a very common and widespread leaf warbler which breeds throughout northern and temperate Europe and the Palearctic, from Ireland east to the Anadyr River basin in eastern Siberia. It is strongly migratory, with almost all of the population wintering in sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Phylloscopus collybita
children.description: The common chiffchaff, or simply the chiffchaff, is a common and widespread leaf warbler which breeds in open woodlands throughout northern and temperate Europe and the Palearctic.

children.name: Phylloscopus sibilatrix
children.description: The wood warbler is a common and widespread leaf warbler which breeds throughout northern and temperate Europe, and just into the extreme west of Asian Russia in the southern Ural Mountains. It is strongly migratory and the entire population winters in tropical Africa.

children.name: Phylloscopus borealis
children.description: The Arctic warbler is a widespread leaf warbler in birch or mixed birch forest near water throughout its breeding range in Fennoscandia and the northern Palearctic. It has established a foothold in North America, breeding in Alaska. This warbler is strongly migratory; the entire population winters in southeast Asia.

children.name: Phylloscopus abietinus
children.description: A pale, cold-toned chiffchaff breeding in boreal spruce and birch forests from Scandinavia east to western Siberia. Long treated as a subspecies of Common Chiffchaff but distinct in plumage and genetics. Winters in northeast Africa, mainly Ethiopia and Sudan.

children.name: Phylloscopus fuscatus
children.description: The dusky warbler is a leaf warbler which breeds in the east Palearctic. The genus name Phylloscopus is from Ancient Greek phullon, "leaf", and skopos, "seeker". The specific fuscatus is from Latin fuscus "dark".

children.name: Phylloscopus fuligiventer
children.description: The smoky warbler (Phylloscopus fuligiventer) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Phylloscopidae.

children.name: Phylloscopus ibericus
children.description: The Iberian chiffchaff (Phylloscopus ibericus) is a species of passerine belonging to the family Phylloscopidae, the leaf warblers.

children.name: Phylloscopus inornatus
children.description: The yellow-browed warbler is a leaf warbler which breeds in the east Palearctic. This warbler is strongly migratory and winters mainly in tropical South Asia and South-east Asia, but also in small numbers in western Europe. Like the rest of Phylloscopidae, it was formerly included in the Old World warbler assemblage.

children.name: Phylloscopus lorenzii
children.description: The common chiffchaff (Phylloscopus collybita), or simply the chiffchaff, is a common and widespread leaf warbler which breeds in open woodlands throughout northern and temperate Europe and the Palearctic.

children.name: Phylloscopus nitidus
children.description: The green warbler (Phylloscopus nitidus), also known as green willow warbler or green leaf warbler, is a leaf warbler found in the Caucasus Mountains in southeastern Europe.

children.name: Phylloscopus proregulus
children.description: Pallas's leaf warbler or Pallas's warbler is a bird that breeds in mountain forests from southern Siberia east to northern Mongolia and northeast China. It is named after the German zoologist Peter Simon Pallas, who first formally described it. This leaf warbler is strongly migratory, wintering mainly in south China and adjacent areas of southeast Asia, although in recent decades increasing numbers have been found in Europe in autumn.

children.name: Phylloscopus sindianus
children.description: The mountain chiffchaff or eastern chiffchaff (Phylloscopus sindianus) is a species of leaf warbler found in the Caucasus (P.

children.name: Phylloscopus tristis
children.description: Siberian chiffchaff (Phylloscopus collybita tristis) is a leaf-warbler which is usually considered a subspecies of the common chiffchaff, but may be a species in its own right.

children.name: Phylloscopus trochiloides
children.description: The greenish warbler is a widespread leaf warbler with a breeding range in northeastern Europe, and temperate to subtropical continental Asia. This warbler is strongly migratory and winters in India. It is not uncommon as a spring or early autumn vagrant in Western Europe and is annually seen in Great Britain.

children.name: Phylloscopus caucasicus
children.description: A pale chiffchaff of the Caucasus mountains and adjacent Turkey, separated from Common Chiffchaff by subtle vocal differences and a more restricted breeding range. One of several taxa in the P. collybita complex that have been successively elevated to species status as fieldwork and genetics advance. Winters in northeast Africa.

children.name: Phylloscopus neumanni
children.description: An African leaf warbler of highland forests in Cameroon and Nigeria, named after the German ornithologist Oscar Neumann who collected extensively in Africa in the late 19th century. Part of a complex of Afromontane Phylloscopus whose relationships have only recently been clarified through genetic studies.

children.name: Seicercus
children.description: Flycatcher-warblers — a genus of small, often colourful leaf warblers formerly placed in Seicercus but now absorbed into Phylloscopidae. Distinguished from typical Phylloscopus by broader bills, shorter wings, and a tendency to flycatch insects on the wing as well as glean from foliage. The group reaches its greatest diversity in the Himalayas and Chinese mountain forests.

children.name: Seicercus grammiceps
children.description: The Sunda warbler (Phylloscopus grammiceps) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Phylloscopidae.

children.name: Acridotheres
children.description: Mynas — robust, conspicuous starlings of South and Southeast Asia renowned for their intelligence, bold temperament, and exceptional vocal abilities. The common myna is among the most successful bird species on the planet, having been introduced to dozens of countries worldwide and listed among the world's 100 worst invasive alien species. Mynas are aggressive competitors for nest cavities and food resources, yet also serve important ecological roles as seed dispersers and insect controllers. Their loud, varied calls and capacity for mimicry have made them popular cage birds for millennia.

children.name: Acridotheres tristis
children.description: The common myna or Indian myna (Acridotheres tristis), sometimes spelled mynah, is a bird in the family Sturnidae, native to Asia.

children.name: Acridotheres fuscus
children.description: The jungle myna (Acridotheres fuscus) is a myna, a member of the starling family.

children.name: Acridotheres grandis
children.description: The great myna (Acridotheres grandis), also known as the white-vented myna, is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Acridotheres cristatellus
children.description: The crested myna (Acridotheres cristatellus), also known as the Chinese starling, is a species of starling in the genus Acridotheres native to southeastern China and Indochina.

children.name: Acridotheres javanicus
children.description: The Javan myna (Acridotheres javanicus), also known as the white-vented myna, is a species of myna in the starling family Sturnidae.

children.name: Acridotheres albocinctus
children.description: The collared myna (Acridotheres albocinctus) is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Acridotheres burmannicus
children.description: The Burmese myna (Acridotheres burmannicus) is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Acridotheres ater
children.description: A black myna with white wing patches from Myanmar and Thailand.

children.name: Acridotheres cinereus
children.description: The pale-bellied myna is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae. It is endemic to the southwestern peninsula of Sulawesi, Indonesia. It has been introduced to Tawau, Sabah (Borneo).

children.name: Acridotheres malayanus
children.description: A myna of the Thai-Malay peninsula and Sumatra, with a short crest and orange bill.

children.name: Ampeliceps
children.description: A monotypic Asian genus containing the golden-crested myna, a striking medium-sized myna of mainland Southeast Asia. The male's brilliant golden-yellow crown and facial patches contrast vividly with its otherwise black plumage, making it one of the most immediately recognisable mynas of the region. It inhabits moist broadleaved forest and forest edge from northeast India through Myanmar and Thailand to Indochina.

children.name: Aplonis
children.description: Pacific starlings — a diverse radiation of mostly plain, dark-plumaged starlings distributed across the Indo-Pacific from South and Southeast Asia to Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia. They include both widespread and abundant species and some of the most range-restricted island endemics in the avian world, with several species having gone extinct in recent centuries due to introduced predators, habitat destruction, and hunting. Their glossy black or dark greenish plumage with bright red or yellow eyes is typical of the group.

children.name: Aplonis atrifusca
children.description: The Samoan starling (Aplonis atrifusca) is a large starling of the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Aplonis cantoroides
children.description: The singing starling (Aplonis cantoroides) is a medium-sized (20 cm in length) starling.

children.name: Aplonis cinerascens
children.description: The Rarotonga starling is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae. It is endemic to Rarotonga in the Cook Islands.

children.name: Aplonis corvina
children.description: The Kosrae starling, also known as Kosrae Island starling, and formerly as Kusaie Mountain starling, (Aplonis corvina) is an extinct bird from the family of starlings (Sturnidae).

children.name: Aplonis feliensis
children.description: A starling from Rennell Island in the Solomons.

children.name: Aplonis insolens
children.description: A starling from the Cook Islands.

children.name: Aplonis mavornata
children.description: The Mauke starling or mysterious starling (Aplonis mavornata) is an extinct species of starling found on the island of Mauke, Cook Islands.

children.name: Aplonis metallica
children.description: The metallic starling (Aplonis metallica), also known as the shining starling, is a bird in the starling family native to the Moluccas, New Guinea, Queensland and the Solomon Islands.

children.name: Aplonis opaca
children.description: The Micronesian starling (Aplonis opaca) is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Aplonis pelzelni
children.description: The Pohnpei starling (Aplonis pelzelni), also known as Pohnpei mountain starling or Ponape mountain starling, is an extremely rare or possibly extinct bird from the family of starlings (Sturnidae).

children.name: Aplonis santovestris
children.description: The mountain starling (Aplonis santovestris), also known as Vanuatu starling, Santo mountain starling or Santo starling, is a bird species in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Aplonis striata
children.description: The striated starling (Aplonis striata) is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Aplonis tabuensis
children.description: The Polynesian starling (Aplonis tabuensis) is a species of starling of the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Basilornis
children.description: Basilornis — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Cinnyricinclus
children.description: Violet-backed starlings — small, sexually dimorphic African starlings in which males are among the most visually spectacular passerines on the continent. The male's upperparts are a dazzling, almost holographic violet-purple, reflecting light like polished metal; females and immatures are brown and streaked, so different as to appear a separate species. The violet-backed starling is a migratory woodland species that performs spectacular aerial displays; it moves seasonally across sub-Saharan Africa following rains and fruiting events.

children.name: Creatophora
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the wattled starling, a remarkable African starling known for the extraordinary seasonal transformation of breeding males. Outside the breeding season the wattled starling is a plain, greyish-brown bird, but during breeding males develop highly conspicuous bright yellow and black wattles on the head and become partially bald, one of the most dramatic breeding adornments among starlings. It is a nomadic, locust-following species of open grasslands and savanna across sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Creatophora cinerea
children.description: The wattled starling (Creatophora cinerea) is a nomadic resident bird in eastern and southern Africa.

children.name: Enodes
children.description: Enodes — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Enodes erythrophris
children.description: The fiery-browed starling or fiery-browed myna is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae. It is monotypic within the genus Enodes. Distinguished by a reddish-orange stripe over the eye, it is endemic to the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, mainly living in humid highland forest.

children.name: Fregilupus
children.description: Fregilupus — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Gracula
children.description: Hill mynas — large, glossy black mynas of South and Southeast Asia celebrated as among the finest avian mimics in the world. The hill myna's ability to reproduce human speech with remarkable fidelity of tone, pitch, and timbre has made it the quintessential cage bird of Asia and a favourite the world over. In the wild these birds inhabit tropical forest canopy, living in small noisy flocks and producing a remarkable repertoire of loud whistles, screams, and gurgles that carry far through dense forest. Orange-yellow facial wattles and white wing patches are characteristic of the genus.

children.name: Gracula religiosa
children.description: The common hill myna (Gracula religiosa), sometimes spelled "mynah" and formerly simply known as the hill myna or myna bird, is a species of starling found in the hills of South and Southeast Asia.

children.name: Gracula indica
children.description: The southern hill myna (Gracula indica) is a member of the starling family.

children.name: Gracula robusta
children.description: The common hill myna (Gracula religiosa), sometimes spelled "mynah" and formerly simply known as the hill myna or myna bird, is a species of starling found in the hills of South and Southeast Asia.

children.name: Gracula enganensis
children.description: The common hill myna (Gracula religiosa), sometimes spelled "mynah" and formerly simply known as the hill myna or myna bird, is a species of starling found in the hills of South and Southeast Asia.

children.name: Gracula pitilogenys
children.description: Endemic to Sri Lanka's wet zone forests. Distinguished from G. indica by its shorter, less bulky yellow wattles. Listed as Endangered by habitat loss.

children.name: Gracula strenua
children.description: A large hill myna endemic to Enggano Island, Indonesia. Its massive bill and distinct vocalisations set it apart from other Gracula species.

children.name: Gracula engannoensis
children.description: A recently recognised species from Enggano Island, differing from G. religiosa in its larger size and yellow wattles covering more of the crown.

children.name: Gracula picta
children.description: A hill myna of Enggano Island with a distinctive colour pattern.

children.name: Gracula temuchii
children.description: A distinctive and well-known species within its range. It inhabits a variety of habitats from lowland forests to mountain highlands, feeding on insects, seeds, and fruits.

children.name: Grafisia
children.description: Grafisia — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Lamprotornis
children.description: Glossy starlings — a spectacular radiation of iridescent African starlings whose plumage reflects structural colours of breathtaking intensity: metallic blues, greens, purples, and bronzes that shift with the angle of light. These are among the most visually striking passerines on Earth, common across sub-Saharan Africa in habitats from dense forest to open savanna. Many species are familiar and abundant birds at African lodges and campsites, their liquid whistles and clanging calls among the most characteristic sounds of the African bush. Several long-tailed species are among the most ornate birds in the family.

children.name: Gracula temuchii
children.description: A hill myna of the Sulu Archipelago in the Philippines.

children.name: Lamprotornis aeneus
children.description: A glossy starling of West African savannas with a bronze-green tail.

children.name: Lamprotornis albicinctus
children.description: A glossy starling of East African highlands with a white collar.

children.name: Lamprotornis bicolor
children.description: The pied starling or African pied starling (Lamprotornis bicolor) is a bird endemic to South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini.

children.name: Lamprotornis cupreocaudus
children.description: A glossy starling with a copper-coloured tail, found in Central Africa.

children.name: Lamprotornis nitens
children.description: , South Africa]] The Cape starling (Lamprotornis nitens), also known as red-shouldered glossy-starling or Cape glossy starling, is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Lamprotornis ornatus
children.description: The Principe starling (Lamprotornis ornatus), also known as the Príncipe glossy-starling, is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Lamprotornis purpureus
children.description: thumb|right|A purple starling at Birdworld, UK.

children.name: Lamprotornis splendidus
children.description: The splendid starling (Lamprotornis splendidus), also known as the splendid glossy-starling, is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Lamprotornis superbus
children.description: The superb starling (Lamprotornis superbus) is a member of the starling family of birds.

children.name: Lamprotornis unicolor
children.description: The ashy starling (Lamprotornis unicolor) is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Lamprotornis violacior
children.description: A distinctive and well-known species within its range. It inhabits a variety of habitats from lowland forests to mountain highlands, feeding on insects, seeds, and fruits.

children.name: Leucopsar
children.description: Pure white starlings with striking bare blue facial skin; one of the most endangered birds in the world.

children.name: Leucopsar rothschildi
children.description: The Bali myna (Leucopsar rothschildi), also known as Rothschild's mynah, Bali starling, or Bali mynah, locally known as jalak Bali, is a medium-sized (up to long), stocky myna native to northeast Bali in Indonesia.

children.name: Mino
children.description: Yellow-faced mynas — large, colourful mynas of New Guinea and adjacent islands with vivid bare yellow facial skin and bold black-and-yellow or black-and-orange plumage. They are among the most conspicuous birds of New Guinea's forest canopy, their loud calls carrying far through the dense vegetation. Like the hill mynas of Gracula, they are celebrated for their vocal abilities and are popular cage birds across Southeast Asia and in aviculture worldwide.

children.name: Mino anais
children.description: The golden myna (Mino anais) is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Necropsar
children.description: Necropsar — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Neocichla
children.description: Neocichla — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Onychognathus
children.description: Chestnut-winged starlings — a group of large, robust African starlings whose males are predominantly glossy blue-black or purplish with conspicuous chestnut primary patches visible in flight. The females of most species are grey-headed or paler, providing striking sexual dichromatism. They are generally birds of rocky country, cliffs, and mountains, nesting on ledges and in crevices rather than in tree cavities. The red-winged starling is a familiar and bold bird of African cities, nesting on buildings and cliff faces alike.

children.name: Pastor
children.description: Rosy starlings — striking, irruptive starlings of the central Asian steppes whose periodic westward irruptions bring them to Sweden as rare but unmistakeable vagrants. The rosy starling (rosenstare) is one of the most immediately recognisable birds on a Swedish list: its vivid combination of bubblegum pink body and glossy black head, wings, and tail makes it impossible to confuse with anything else.
