Like many nomadic steppe birds it irrupts westward irregularly, following locust swarms that erupt on the Eurasian steppes — the birds follow the locusts and can appear anywhere in western Europe and Scandinavia during such events. It is one of the most sought-after vagrants for Swedish birdwatchers, and years of irruption can bring tens of individuals to the country.

children.name: Pastor roseus
children.description: The rosy starling, also known as the rose-coloured starling or rose-coloured pastor, is a passerine bird in the starling family. The species was recently placed in its own monotypic genus, Pastor, and split from Sturnus. This split is supported by recent studies, though other related species within its new genus are not yet known for certain.

children.name: Poeoptera
children.description: Poeoptera — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Proterothrix
children.description: Proterothrix — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Rhabdornis
children.description: Rhabdornis — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Sarcops
children.description: Sarcops — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Sarcops calvus
children.description: The coleto is a starling species in the monotypic genus Sarcops. It is endemic to the Philippines. Its natural habitats are tropical dry forest, tropical moist lowland forest, and tropical moist montane forest.

children.name: Saroglossa
children.description: A monotypic Asian genus containing the spot-winged starling, a medium-sized starling of the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. Males have distinctive rufous underparts and a spotted wing pattern; females are duller. It inhabits broadleaved forest and forest edge, often visiting flowering trees for nectar and small fruit.

children.name: Scissirostrum
children.description: A monotypic Indonesian genus containing the finch-billed starling (or grosbeak starling), notable for its unusually heavy, finch-like bill that is quite unlike the slender bill of most starlings. It is endemic to Sulawesi and adjacent islands, where it is a colonial breeder excavating cavities in dead wood. It feeds heavily on seeds, using its robust bill to dehusk tough grain — an unusual dietary specialisation among starlings.

children.name: Scissirostrum dubium
children.description: The grosbeak starling (Scissirostrum dubium), also known as the grosbeak myna, finch-billed myna, or scissor-billed starling, is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Speculipastor
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the magpie starling, a striking black-and-white starling of arid East Africa. With its pied pattern and long tail it superficially recalls a magpie, hence its English name. It inhabits dry open country and Acacia–Commiphora scrubland from Ethiopia and Somalia south through Kenya, nesting in termite mounds or tree cavities.

children.name: Speculipastor bicolor
children.description: The magpie starling (Speculipastor bicolor) is a member of the starling family from eastern Africa.

children.name: Speculipastor
children.description: A striking black-and-white starling of arid East Africa with a long tail and pied plumage.

children.name: Speculipastor bicolor
children.description: The magpie starling (Speculipastor bicolor) is a member of the starling family from eastern Africa.

children.name: Streptocitta
children.description: Streptocitta — a genus of starlings in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Sturnus
children.description: European starlings — extraordinarily social, adaptable, and vocally accomplished passerines that were once one of the most numerous farmland birds in northern Europe. The common starling (stare) is famous above all for its murmurations: in autumn, flocks of tens of thousands — sometimes hundreds of thousands — perform breathtaking coordinated aerial displays over Swedish wetlands, particularly at pre-roost gatherings in reedbeds. The intricate, unpredictable shape-shifting of murmuration flocks — a phenomenon studied by physicists using techniques from statistical mechanics — emerges from each bird following just six or seven of its nearest neighbours, with no central coordination. The starling is also one of Sweden's greatest mimics, incorporating the calls of other species, mechanical sounds, and even human speech into its continuous, churring song. Despite its familiarity, the starling is a rapidly declining farmland species throughout Sweden and Europe.

children.name: Sturnus vulgaris
children.description: The common starling, also known simply as the starling in Great Britain and Ireland, and as the European starling in North America, is a medium-sized passerine bird in the starling family, Sturnidae. It is about 20 cm (8 in) long and has glossy black plumage with a metallic sheen, which is speckled with white at some times of the year. The legs are pink and the bill is black in winter and yellow in summer; young birds have browner plumage than the adults.

children.name: Sturnus unicolor
children.description: The spotless starling is a passerine bird in the starling family, Sturnidae. It is closely related to the common starling, but has a much more restricted range, confined to the Iberian Peninsula, Northwest Africa, southernmost France, and the islands of Sicily, Corsica and Sardinia. It is largely non-migratory.

children.name: Sturnus burmannicus
children.description: The Burmese myna (Acridotheres burmannicus) is a species of starling in the family Sturnidae.

children.name: Sturnus eremicus
children.description: A starling of the arid coastal plains of Somalia and Djibouti; grey-brown with a pale belly and a black mask. Often found foraging on the ground near livestock.

children.name: Sturnus neglectus
children.description: A medium-sized starling of the Middle East and Central Asia, with a notably glossy green and purple sheen. The specific name reflects its former obscurity when treated as a subspecies of the common starling.

children.name: Sturnus opacus
children.description: A winter visitor to the Indian subcontinent from Central Asia. Its plumage is more uniformly dark than that of the European starling, lacking the white spots of the breeding plumage.

children.name: Sturnus caucasicus
children.description: A large, purple-glossed starling of the Caucasus and northern Iran. Its plumage has a notably strong purple sheen compared to the green gloss of the European starling.

children.name: Sturnus sturninus
children.description: The Daurian starling (Agropsar sturninus), or purple-backed starling, is a species of bird in the starling family found in the eastern Palearctic from eastern Mongolia and southeastern Russia to North Korea and central China.

children.name: Sturnus pagodarum
children.description: The brahminy starling or brahminy myna (Sturnia pagodarum) is a member of the starling family of birds.

children.name: Sturnus albifrons
children.description: Sturnus albifrons (White-faced Starling) is a european starlings species found in Asia region.

children.name: Acrocephalus
children.description: Reed warblers — quintessential summer birds of reedbeds and marshy scrub across the Old World, combining remarkable vocal complexity with cryptic brown plumage and elusive habits that make them far more often heard than seen. The family name derives from Greek for 'pointed head', reflecting the flattened crown that gives these birds a characteristic profile as they slip through reed stems. The genus spans from Eurasian breeding species that winter in Africa to island endemics of the Pacific, Mascarene islands, and Indian Ocean.

children.name: Acrocephalus scirpaceus
children.description: The common reed warbler or Eurasian reed-warbler is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus. It breeds across Europe into the temperate western Palaearctic where it is migratory, wintering in sub-Saharan Africa. It is also a resident species over large parts of Africa.

children.name: Acrocephalus arundinaceus
children.description: The great reed warbler is an insectivorous bird in the family Acrocephalidae. It is a medium-sized passerine bird and the largest of the warblers. It breeds throughout mainland Europe and the Western Palearctic and migrates to sub-Saharan Africa in the winter.

children.name: Acrocephalus palustris
children.description: The marsh warbler is an Old World warbler currently classified in the family Acrocephalidae. It breeds in temperate Europe and the western Palearctic and winters mainly in southeast Africa. It is notable for incorporating striking imitations of a wide variety of other birds into its song.

children.name: Acrocephalus melanopogon
children.description: The moustached warbler (Acrocephalus melanopogon) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus schoenobaenus
children.description: The sedge warbler is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus. It is a medium-sized warbler with a brown, streaked back and wings and a distinct pale supercilium. Sedge warblers are migratory, crossing the Sahara to get from their European and Asian breeding grounds to spend winter in Africa.

children.name: Acrocephalus dumetorum
children.description: Blyth's reed warbler is a species of reed warbler belonging to the family Acrocephalidae, which also includes the tree warblers. Blyth's reed warbler breeds across the Palearctic zoogeographical region and winters in South Asia. The species has been expanding its range westwards in Europe.

children.name: Acrocephalus stentoreus
children.description: The clamorous reed warbler (Acrocephalus stentoreus) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus baeticatus
children.description: The common reed warbler or Eurasian reed-warbler (Acrocephalus scirpaceus) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus agricola
children.description: The paddyfield warbler is a species of marsh warbler. It was formerly included in the "Old World warbler" assemblage. The Manchurian reed warbler was included in A.

children.name: Acrocephalus paludicola
children.description: ]] The aquatic warbler (Acrocephalus paludicola) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus scirpaceus fuscus
children.description: Sometimes treated as a full species, this eastern form of the Eurasian reed warbler breeds around the Caspian Sea and in Central Asia east to Afghanistan, and is slightly smaller and greyer than the nominate western population. Recent genetic work supports treating it as a separate species, Acrocephalus fuscus, though this treatment remains contested. It winters in East Africa and differs subtly in vocalisation and morphology from western scirpaceus.

children.name: Acrocephalus caffer
children.description: The Tahiti reed warbler (Acrocephalus caffer) is a songbird in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus cinnamomeus
children.description: The common reed warbler or Eurasian reed-warbler (Acrocephalus scirpaceus) is an Old World warbler in the genus Acrocephalus.

children.name: Acrocephalus immacula
children.description: A small, plain reed warbler endemic to Rodrigues Island in the Mascarenes, now extinct, known only from sub-fossil bones and historical accounts. It likely occupied reed beds and scrub along the island's watercourses before habitat destruction and introduced predators (particularly rats and cats) drove it to extinction, probably in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. Its bones were described in conjunction with the many other Rodrigues extinction-era fauna; it may have survived long enough to be observed by early settlers but was never formally collected.

children.name: Hippolais
children.description: Hippolais warblers — medium-sized, active warblers of scrub and garden habitats with loud, complex songs that include mimicry of other species. The icterine warbler (härmsångare) is the most familiar member of the genus in Sweden: a yellow-green bird with a distinctively angular, peaked crown that breeds in parks, gardens, and mixed woodland edge throughout the country. Its song is a rich, tumbling medley of musical phrases, harsh notes, and imitated sounds delivered with great energy from prominent perches — one of the most complex and attractive warbler songs in Sweden. The Swedish name härmsångare ('mimic singer') perfectly captures the bird's talent for weaving snatches of other species' songs into its own performance.

children.name: Hippolais icterina
children.description: The icterine warbler is an Old World warbler in the tree warbler genus Hippolais. It breeds in mainland Europe except the southwest, where it is replaced by its western counterpart, the melodious warbler. It is migratory, wintering in sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Hippolais polyglotta
children.description: The melodious warbler (Hippolais polyglotta) is an Old World warbler in the tree warbler genus Hippolais.

children.name: Hippolais pallida
children.description: The eastern olivaceous warbler (Iduna pallida), known simply as the olivaceous warbler when its western relative is referred to as the 'isabelline warbler', is a small passerine bird with drab plumage tones, that is native to the Old World.

children.name: Hippolais opaca
children.description: The western olivaceous warbler (Iduna opaca), also known as the isabelline warbler, is a "warbler", formerly placed in the Old World warblers when these were a paraphyletic wastebin taxon.

children.name: Iduna
children.description: Iduna warblers — a group of small to medium-sized unstreaked warblers split from Hippolais following phylogenetic work showing they form a separate clade. They span Africa and Asia, typically inhabiting dry scrub, acacia thickets, and semi-arid scrubland, and share a general brownish-grey plumage with subtle differences in supercilium prominence, bill length, and tail-wagging behaviour. Several are part of a species complex whose boundaries remain debated.

children.name: Iduna caligata
children.description: The booted warbler is a species of passerine bird belonging to the family Acrocephalidae, the reed and tree warblers. This species breeds in Eastern Europe and western Asia, wintering in south Asia. it is a regular vagrant to Western Europe.

children.name: Iduna pallida
children.description: The eastern olivaceous warbler (Iduna pallida), known simply as the olivaceous warbler when its western relative is referred to as the 'isabelline warbler', is a small passerine bird with drab plumage tones, that is native to the Old World.

children.name: Iduna opaca
children.description: The western olivaceous warbler (Iduna opaca), also known as the isabelline warbler, is a "warbler", formerly placed in the Old World warblers when these were a paraphyletic wastebin taxon.

children.name: Iduna nana
children.description: The smallest member of the genus, a delicate, pale warbler of semi-arid scrub, tamarisk and low thorn-bush from Kazakhstan and Central Asia south to northwestern India. Its specific epithet nana refers to its diminutive size. It is an active, tail-flicking species that sings a faint, rapid song from within dense low cover; its song is easily overlooked. The species winters in the Indian subcontinent and is very rarely recorded outside its core Central Asian and South Asian range.

children.name: Iduna languida
children.description: A large Iduna of freshwater marshes, reed beds and riverside vegetation in the Middle East, breeding in the marshes of Iraq and Iran and wintering in East Africa. It is one of the least-known members of the family, with limited data on its population size, though it was historically common in the extensive Mesopotamian marshes. The draining of the Iraqi marshes in the 1990s devastated its core breeding habitat, though partial restoration since 2003 has allowed some recovery. Larger and heavier than most congeners.

children.name: Chloropeta
children.description: African yellow warblers — a small genus of brightly coloured warblers endemic to sub-Saharan Africa, occupying tall grass, papyrus, reed beds, and forest edges near water. Their yellow underparts and greenish-olive upperparts make them among the most distinctively coloured members of the family, contrasting sharply with the drab browns of most Acrocephalus. They are closely associated with tall marsh vegetation and can be remarkably skulking despite their bright plumage.

children.name: Calamonastides
children.description: A monotypic genus containing a single distinctive African reed warbler, related to Acrocephalus but placed in its own genus based on morphological and molecular distinctiveness. It inhabits papyrus swamps and reed beds in East Africa.

children.name: Calamocichla
children.description: African swamp warblers — a genus of large, heavily built reed warblers from sub-Saharan Africa, formerly placed within Acrocephalus. They occupy papyrus swamps, reed beds and tall riverine vegetation and are among the most robust members of the family. Their loud, churring songs are prominent in African wetland soundscapes.

children.name: Calamocichla rufescens
children.description: A large, dark brown swamp warbler specialising in papyrus and tall reed beds across central and East Africa, from Senegal east to Kenya and south to Angola. It is a prominent papyrus-zone bird whose loud, churring song is one of the defining sounds of lowland African swamps. Notably sedentary, it is reluctant to cross open water between swamp fragments, leading to population isolation across the papyrus archipelago of the Congo basin and Albertine Rift.

children.name: Calamocichla gracilirostris
children.description: Africa's most widespread and common swamp warbler, occupying papyrus, Phragmites reed beds, and tall sedge beds from Ethiopia south to South Africa. It shows considerable subspecific variation across its extensive range and has a rich, bubbling song that is a familiar wetland sound across the continent. An important Cuculus cuckoo host in many parts of Africa, with cuckoo egg mimicry having co-evolved with local warbler egg colouration in some populations.

children.name: Calamocichla lopezi
children.description: A montane swamp warbler restricted to highland marshes and bog edges in the Cameroon highlands and Bioko Island in the Gulf of Guinea, at elevations above 1,500 m. It inhabits rank grass, bracken, and sedge at bog margins rather than lowland papyrus, reflecting a distinct altitudinal niche from its congeners. Poorly known and seldom observed, it was long treated as a race of the greater swamp warbler but differs in size, structure and song from lowland relatives.

children.name: Nesillas
children.description: Malagasy brush warblers — a genus of five secretive, long-tailed warblers endemic to Madagascar and the Comoro Islands, occupying dense undergrowth in humid forest, coastal scrub, and degraded vegetation. They are among the most elusive passerines in Madagascar, far more often heard than seen, creeping through dense vegetation like diminutive bush-warblers. Their taxonomy has been revised several times and their relationships within Acrocephalidae are still being clarified.

children.name: Nesillas aldabranus
children.description: Declared extinct in the 1980s, the Aldabra brush warbler was known from a tiny area of dense coastal scrub on Aldabra Atoll, Seychelles. It was last recorded in 1983, and despite the protected status of Aldabra — a UNESCO World Heritage Site — the species could not be saved, likely succumbing to introduced cats and black rats. It is one of the few twentieth-century extinctions of a bird on a currently well-protected island, highlighting how quickly small populations can collapse even in reserves.

children.name: Bebrornis
children.description: Indian Ocean island warblers — a small genus of reed warblers from the Seychelles and Rodrigues, sometimes merged into Acrocephalus. Both species are highly threatened island endemics that have been subjects of intensive conservation intervention, with the Seychelles warbler becoming a celebrated case study in island bird recovery.

children.name: Bebrornis rodericanus
children.description: The Rodrigues warbler (Acrocephalus rodericanus) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Acrocephalidae.

children.name: Bebrornis sechellensis
children.description: The Seychelles warbler (Acrocephalus sechellensis), also known as Seychelles brush warbler, is a small songbird found on five granitic and corraline islands in the Seychelles.

children.name: Amphilais
children.description: A monotypic genus containing a single secretive Malagasy warbler of rank grass and scrub, whose affinities within Acrocephalidae were debated until molecular work confirmed its placement. Like Nesillas, it is an elusive ground-level creeper of Madagascar's humid habitats.

children.name: Amphilais seebohmi
children.description: The grey emutail (Bradypterus seebohmi), also known as the Madagascan grassbird or feather-tailed warbler, is an emutail in the family Locustellidae.

children.name: Thamnornis
children.description: A monotypic genus of Madagascar, containing a single species of dry forest and spiny scrub. The genus was long of uncertain family placement but is now confirmed in Acrocephalidae. It occupies the unique xerophytic habitats of southwestern Madagascar.

children.name: Randia
children.description: A monotypic genus of Madagascar, recently described and recognised as a distinct genus within Acrocephalidae. It inhabits dry forests and the ecotone between humid and dry zones in Madagascar.

children.name: Regulus
children.description: Kinglets and firecrests — Europe's and North America's smallest birds, weighing as little as 5 grams yet capable of surviving Scandinavian winters in spruce forest by constant foraging through the night. The goldcrest (kungsfågel — 'king bird') takes its royal name from the brilliant gold and orange crown stripe that is erected into a crest during display and aggressive encounters: the English 'goldcrest' and Latin Regulus ('little king') both reflect this crown. The goldcrest breeds in almost every Swedish spruce forest and migrates in vast numbers each autumn, moving in loose mixed flocks with tits through the coastal zone; in some years hundreds of thousands cross the Swedish coast on a single October day. The firecrest, with its additional white supercilium and blazing orange crown, is slowly expanding northward into southern Sweden as temperatures warm.

children.name: Regulus regulus
children.description: The goldcrest is a very small passerine bird in the kinglet family. Its colourful golden crest feathers, as well as being called the "king of the birds" in European folklore, gives rise to its English and scientific names. The scientific name, R.

children.name: Regulus ignicapilla
children.description: The common firecrest (Regulus ignicapilla), also known as the firecrest, is a very small passerine bird in the kinglet family.

children.name: Regulus teneriffae
children.description: The Tenerife goldcrest (Regulus regulus teneriffae) is a subspecies of the goldcrest.

children.name: Regulus madeirensis
children.description: The Madeira firecrest, Madeira kinglet, or Madeiracrest (Regulus madeirensis) is a very small passerine bird endemic to the island of Madeira.

children.name: Sylvia
children.description: Scrub warblers of hedgerows, thickets, and forest edge. The Blackcap is one of Sweden's finest songsters, a rich outpouring of clear fluted notes; the Common Whitethroat perches conspicuously on bramble tops to deliver its scratchy, cheerful song.

children.name: Sylvia atricapilla
children.description: The Eurasian blackcap is a bird usually known simply as the blackcap. It is a common and widespread warbler. It has mainly olive-grey upperparts and pale grey underparts, and differences across the five subspecies are small.

children.name: Sylvia borin
children.description: The garden warbler (Sylvia borin) is a common and widespread small bird that breeds in most of Europe and in the Palearctic to western Siberia.

children.name: Sylvia communis
children.description: The common whitethroat or greater whitethroat (Curruca communis) is a common and widespread Old World warbler which breeds throughout Europe and across much of temperate western Asia.

children.name: Sylvia curruca
children.description: The lesser whitethroat (Curruca curruca) is a common and widespread Old World warbler which breeds in temperate Europe, except the southwest, and in the western and central Palearctic.

children.name: Sylvia nisoria
children.description: The barred warbler (Curruca nisoria) is a species of bird in the warbler family Sylviidae which breeds across temperate regions of central and eastern Europe and western and central Asia.

children.name: Sylvia melanocephala
children.description: The Sardinian warbler (Curruca melanocephala) is a common and widespread Sylviidae warbler from the Mediterranean region.

children.name: Sylvia undata
children.description: The Dartford warbler (Curruca undata) is a Sylviid warbler from the warmer parts of western Europe and northwestern Africa.

children.name: Sylvia melanothorax
children.description: The Cyprus warbler (Curruca melanothorax) is a warbler species in the family Sylviidae which breeds only on Cyprus.

children.name: Sylvia conspicillata
children.description: The spectacled warbler (Curruca conspicillata) is a species of passerine bird in the warbler genus Curruca in the family Sylviidae.

children.name: Sylvia leucomelaena
children.description: The Arabian warbler (Curruca leucomelaena), also known as Red Sea warbler or Blandford's warbler, is a species of Old World warbler in the family Sylviidae.

children.name: Sylvia balearica
children.description: The Balearic warbler (Curruca balearica) is a warbler species of the genus Curruca.

children.name: Sylvia althaea
children.description: The lesser whitethroat (Curruca curruca) is a common and widespread Old World warbler which breeds in temperate Europe, except the southwest, and in the western and central Palearctic.

children.name: Sylvia minula
children.description: The lesser whitethroat (Curruca curruca) is a common and widespread Old World warbler which breeds in temperate Europe, except the southwest, and in the western and central Palearctic.

children.name: Sylvia margelanica
children.description: The lesser whitethroat (Curruca curruca) is a common and widespread Old World warbler which breeds in temperate Europe, except the southwest, and in the western and central Palearctic.

children.name: Sylvia nana
children.description: thumb|Desert warbler at [[Kutch]] The Asian desert warbler (Curruca nana) is an Old World warbler which breeds in the deserts of central and western Asia and the extreme east of Europe (Volga Delta area east to western Inner Mongolia in China), and migrating to similar habitats in southwestern Asia (Arabia to northwestern India) and the far northeast of Africa (Red Sea coastal regions) in winter.

children.name: Sylvia deserti
children.description: The African desert warbler (Curruca deserti) is a species of warbler in the family Sylviidae.

children.name: Sylvia buryi
children.description: The Yemen warbler or Yemen parisoma (Curruca buryi) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Sylviidae.

children.name: Sylvia lugens
children.description: The brown parisoma or brown warbler (Curruca lugens) is an Old World warbler of the family Sylviidae found in eastern Africa.

children.name: Sylvia galinieri
children.description: The Abyssinian catbird (Sylvia galinieri), also known as the juniper babbler, is a small passerine in the family Sylviidae, endemic to the highland forests and scrub of Ethiopia.

children.name: Sylvia boehmi
children.description: The banded parisoma (Curruca boehmi), banded tit warbler or banded warbler, is a species of Old World warbler in the family Sylviidae.

children.name: Rhopophilus
children.description: The Chinese hill warblers — long-tailed, skulking birds of northern Chinese scrub and hillsides, with a complex, musical song. They were long considered babblers but molecular studies place them firmly within the sylviid radiation.

children.name: Rhopophilus pekinensis
children.description: The Beijing babbler (Rhopophilus pekinensis), also known as the white-browed Chinese warbler, Chinese hill warbler, or Chinese bush-dweller, is a species of bird in the genus Rhopophilus.

children.name: Rhopophilus albosuperciliaris
children.description: The Tarim babbler (Rhopophilus albosuperciliaris), also known as the Tarim hill warbler is a species of bird in the genus Rhopophilus.

children.name: Chrysomma
children.description: Yellow-eyed babblers — small, warm-brown birds of tall grasslands and reeds in South and Southeast Asia, with bright orange-yellow irises and a habit of creeping through dense stems like mice.

children.name: Fulvetta
children.description: Fulvettas — small, brownish babblers of Asian montane forests, formerly placed with the laughingthrushes but now recognised as sylviid warblers. They are active, gregarious foragers in the understorey and bamboo thickets.

children.name: Fulvetta formosana
children.description: The Taiwan fulvetta (Fulvetta formosana) is a species of bird in the family Sylviidae.

children.name: Fulvetta danisi
children.description: The Indochinese fulvetta (Fulvetta danisi) is a bird species in the family Paradoxornithidae.

children.name: Fulvetta manipurensis
children.description: The Manipur fulvetta or streak-throated fulvetta (Fulvetta manipurensis) is a bird species in the family Paradoxornithidae.

children.name: Fulvetta striaticollis
children.description: The Chinese fulvetta (Fulvetta striaticollis) is a bird species in the family Paradoxornithidae.

children.name: Fulvetta ruficapilla
children.description: The spectacled fulvetta (Fulvetta ruficapilla) is a bird species in the family Paradoxornithidae.

children.name: Fulvetta claudi
children.description: A recently described fulvetta from the mountains of Yunnan in southwestern China, where it inhabits bamboo thickets in montane forest. It is grey-headed with warm brown upperparts.

children.name: Fulvetta sordidior
children.description: A dull-plumaged fulvetta of the eastern Himalayas and Southeast Asian highlands, with a grey head, brown back, and darker throat.

children.name: Fulvetta przewalskii
children.description: A fulvetta from the mountains of western China, with a distinctive white throat and warm brown body. It is poorly known and occupies a restricted range.

children.name: Lioparus
children.description: A monotypic genus for the Golden-breasted Fulvetta — a dazzling little bird of Asian montane bamboo forests with a brilliant golden-yellow breast and a complex, bubbling song.

children.name: Chleuasicus
children.description: Small, stout parrotbills of Asian bamboo and grasslands, with thick finch-like bills adapted for splitting bamboo and grass stems to extract insects and seeds.

children.name: Conostoma
children.description: A monotypic genus for the Great Parrotbill — the largest of all the parrotbills, with a massive, conical yellow bill and a robust, thrush-like body. It inhabits high-altitude bamboo forests.

children.name: Conostoma aemodium
children.description: The great parrotbill (Paradoxornis aemodius) is a bird species the Paradoxornithidae family.

children.name: Moupinia
children.description: A monotypic genus for the Rufous-tailed Babbler, a long-tailed, skulking bird of scrub and thickets in central China with a rich rufous tail and melodious song.

children.name: Myzornis
children.description: A monotypic genus for the Fire-tailed Myzornis — one of the most spectacularly coloured birds in Asia, with vivid green, blue, yellow, black, and red plumage. It forages in mixed-species flocks in the mossy canopy of Himalayan cloud forests.

children.name: Sinosuthora
children.description: Vinous-throated parrotbills — small, active parrotbills of East and Southeast Asian scrub, grassland, and reed-bed, with a short thick bill and soft, vinous-washed plumage. The most widespread members of the parrotbill radiation, moving in restless family parties through dense vegetation.

children.name: Aegithalos
children.description: Tiny tail-heavy birds that move through woodland in chattering flocks. They build one of the most elaborate nests in European ornithology — an oval elastic cocoon of moss and lichen woven with spider silk and lined with hundreds of feathers, expandable as the chicks grow. In hard winters they huddle together for warmth at roost.

children.name: Aegithalos caudatus
children.description: The long-tailed tit or long-tailed bushtit is a common bird species belonging to the bushtit family found throughout Eurasia. An insectivore, it inhabits deciduous and mixed woodlands as well as scrub, heathland, farmland, parks and gardens. The plumage of this small long-tailed bird is predominantly black and white with varying amounts of pink and grey.

children.name: Aegithalos fuliginosus
children.description: The sooty bushtit (Aegithalos fuliginosus), also known as the sooty tit, white-necklaced tit or white-necklaced bushtit, is a small passerine bird in the bushtit family Aegithalidae.

children.name: Psaltria
children.description: A monotypic genus for the pygmy bushtit, the smallest member of the family, endemic to the mountains of Java.

children.name: Psaltria exilis
children.description: The pygmy bushtit (Aegithalos exilis), also called the pygmy tit, is the smallest species of passerine bird.

children.name: Psaltriparus
children.description: A monotypic genus for the American bushtit, the only member of the family in the New World.

children.name: Psaltriparus minimus
children.description: The American bushtit, or simply bushtit (Psaltriparus minimus), is a social songbird belonging to the monotypic genus Psaltriparus.

children.name: Leptopoecile
children.description: The tit-warblers, brilliantly coloured small birds of high Central Asian mountains, washed in violet, blue, and lilac.

children.name: Sitta
children.description: The only birds that routinely walk headfirst down tree trunks, gripping bark with powerful feet and using the bill to lever up bark and extract insects. They wedge nuts in bark crevices to hack them open — hence the name. The Eurasian Nuthatch plasters the entrance of its nest hole with mud to exactly its own body diameter.

children.name: Sitta europaea
children.description: The Eurasian nuthatch, wood nuthatch, or simply nuthatch, is a small passerine bird found throughout the Palearctic and in Europe. Like other nuthatches, it is a short-tailed bird with a long bill, blue-gray upperparts and a black eye-stripe. It is a vocal bird with a repeated loud dwip call.

children.name: Sitta arctica
children.description: The Siberian nuthatch (Sitta arctica) is a bird species of the family Sittidae.

children.name: Sitta cashmirensis
children.description: The Kashmir nuthatch (Sitta cashmirensis) is a species of bird in the family Sittidae.

children.name: Sitta castanea
children.description: The Indian nuthatch (Sitta castanea) is a species of bird in the family Sittidae.

children.name: Sitta neglecta
children.description: The Burmese nuthatch (Sitta neglecta), also known as the neglected nuthatch, is a species of bird in the family Sittidae.

children.name: Sitta azurea
children.description: The blue nuthatch (Sitta azurea) is a bird species in the nuthatch family Sittidae.

children.name: Sitta pygmaea
children.description: The pygmy nuthatch (Sitta pygmaea) is a tiny songbird, native to western North America.

children.name: Sitta insularis
children.description: The Bahama nuthatch (Sitta insularis) is a nuthatch species endemic to the pineyards of Grand Bahama island in the Bahamas.

children.name: Sitta whiteheadi
children.description: The Corsican nuthatch (Sitta whiteheadi) is a species of bird in the nuthatch family Sittidae.

children.name: Sitta ledanti
children.description: The Algerian nuthatch or Kabyle nuthatch (Sitta ledanti) is a species of bird in the nuthatch family Sittidae.

children.name: Sitta villosa
children.description: The Chinese nuthatch or snowy-browed nuthatch (Sitta villosa) is a species of bird in the family Sittidae.

children.name: Sitta yunnanensis
children.description: The Yunnan nuthatch (Sitta yunnanensis) is a bird species in the nuthatch family Sittidae.

children.name: Sitta neumayer
children.description: The western rock nuthatch (Sitta neumayer) is a small passerine bird which breeds from Croatia east through Greece and Turkey to Iran.

children.name: Sitta magna
children.description: The giant nuthatch (Sitta magna) is a species of bird in the family Sittidae.

children.name: Sitta formosa
children.description: The beautiful nuthatch (Sitta formosa) is a bird species in the family Sittidae, collectively known as nuthatches.

children.name: Certhia
children.description: Slender streak-backed birds that spiral up tree trunks like animated pieces of bark, probing crevices with a fine curved bill. They always work upward — once at the top they drop to the base of the next tree and begin again. The two Swedish species are almost identical and best separated by their songs.

children.name: Certhia familiaris
children.description: The Eurasian treecreeper or common treecreeper is a small passerine bird also known in the British Isles, where it is the only living member of its genus, simply as treecreeper. It is similar to other treecreepers, and has a curved bill, patterned brown upperparts, whitish underparts, and long stiff tail feathers which help it creep up tree trunks. It can be most easily distinguished from the similar short-toed treecreeper, which shares much of its European range, by its different song.

children.name: Certhia americana
children.description: The brown creeper (Certhia americana), also known as the American treecreeper, is a small songbird, the only North American member of the treecreeper family Certhiidae.

children.name: Certhia discolor
children.description: The Sikkim treecreeper (Certhia discolor) is a species of bird in the treecreeper family.

children.name: Salpornis
children.description: The spotted creepers, boldly spotted bark-foragers of Africa and India.

children.name: Salpornis spilonotus
children.description: The Indian spotted creeper (Salpornis spilonota) is a small passerine bird that is a member of the family Salpornithidae, which was previously treated as a subfamily of Certhiidae.

children.name: Campylorhynchus
children.description: The largest wrens, boldly patterned with streaked or barred plumage and notably loud, chattering duets. Found from the southwestern United States through Central America and northern South America, often in arid scrub, cactus desert, and forest edge. Several species are highly social and cooperative breeders.

children.name: Campylorhynchus brunneicapillus
children.description: The cactus wren (Campylorhynchus brunneicapillus) is a species of wren that is endemic to the deserts of the southwestern United States and northern and central Mexico.

children.name: Campylorhynchus chiapensis
children.description: The giant wren (Campylorhynchus chiapensis) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Campylorhynchus fasciatus
children.description: The fasciated wren (Campylorhynchus fasciatus) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Campylorhynchus griseus
children.description: The bicolored wren (Campylorhynchus griseus) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Campylorhynchus gularis
children.description: The spotted wren (Campylorhynchus gularis) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Campylorhynchus rufinucha
children.description: The Veracruz wren (Campylorhynchus rufinucha) is a songbird of the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Campylorhynchus unicolor
children.description: A plain grey-brown, unstreaked Campylorhynchus restricted to the cloud forest edges and humid montane scrub of the western Andes in Ecuador and northern Peru. It is the most range-restricted member of its genus and among the least-studied. Its subdued plumage and quiet habits make it easy to overlook.

children.name: Campylorhynchus yucatanicus
children.description: The Yucatan wren (Campylorhynchus yucatanicus) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Campylorhynchus barroti
children.description: A heavily streaked, dark-capped wren of humid foothill and lowland forest in Panama and Colombia. It was long treated as a subspecies of the Band-backed Wren but is now recognised as a full species based on plumage and vocal differences. Like its congeners, it is a cooperative breeder living in extended family groups.

children.name: Salpinctes
children.description: A monotypic genus of rocky desert wrens found throughout the arid interior of western North America. Rock Wrens are highly adapted to life among boulders and cliff faces, where they construct pebble pavements leading to their nests.

children.name: Salpinctes obsoletus
children.description: The rock wren (Salpinctes obsoletus) is a small songbird of the wren family native to the rocky areas of western North America.

children.name: Catherpes
children.description: A monotypic genus of canyon-dwelling wrens with a remarkably long, decurved bill used to probe crevices in cliff faces and rocky outcrops in western North America.

children.name: Catherpes mexicanus
children.description: The canyon wren (Catherpes mexicanus) is a small North American songbird of the wren family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Hylorchilus
children.description: Two rare and poorly known wrens endemic to Mexico, associated with limestone karst outcrops and forested ravines. Both species have restricted ranges and are considered vulnerable or near-threatened.

children.name: Cistothorus
children.description: Marsh and grassland wrens of the Americas, typically skulking in dense vegetation and difficult to observe despite their loud, mechanical songs. Several species are marsh obligates, nesting among cattails and sedges over standing water.

children.name: Cistothorus stellaris
children.description: The sedge wren (Cistothorus stellaris) is a small and secretive passerine bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Cistothorus palustris
children.description: The marsh wren is a small North American songbird of the wren family. It was formerly called the long-billed marsh wren to distinguish it from the sedge wren, then known as the short-billed marsh wren.

children.name: Thryomanes
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Bewick's Wren, a widespread and adaptable wren of western North America known for its exceptionally varied and musical song.

children.name: Thryophilus
children.description: Middle American and northern South American wrens of forest edge and thickets, characterised by warm rufous or brown tones and often bold face patterns. Several species are restricted to narrow geographic ranges.

children.name: Thryophilus sinaloa
children.description: thumb|El Tuito, Jalisco, Mexico thumb|El Tuito, Jalisco, Mexico.

children.name: Thryophilus pleurostictus
children.description: The banded wren (Thryophilus pleurostictus) is a small songbird of the wren family.

children.name: Thryophilus spadix
children.description: A dark-capped, rufous-brown wren of humid lowland and foothill forest in Panama and northwestern Colombia, associated with dense undergrowth near streams and forest edges. It was long considered a subspecies of the Rufous-and-white Wren but differs in its dark sooty-grey head and more restricted range. Its loud duets are characteristic sounds of wet lowland forest.

children.name: Pheugopedius
children.description: A genus of mostly Middle American and northern South American wrens with boldly patterned faces and rich, complex songs. Many species were formerly placed in Thryothorus; molecular analysis prompted a widespread reclassification.

children.name: Pheugopedius genibarbis
children.description: The moustached wren (Pheugopedius genibarbis) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Pheugopedius felix
children.description: The happy wren (Pheugopedius felix) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Pheugopedius mystacalis
children.description: | range_map = Pheugopedius mystacalis map.svg.

children.name: Pheugopedius coraya
children.description: | range_map = Pheugopedius coraya map.svg.

children.name: Pheugopedius schlegelii
children.description: Named after the Dutch ornithologist Hermann Schlegel, this Andean foothills wren ranges from Colombia to Bolivia in humid subtropical and tropical forest undergrowth. Its speckled breast and streaked head distinguish it from similar congeners. It is most often encountered in dense tangled vegetation along forest borders and ravines.

children.name: Pheugopedius solstitialis
children.description: A richly streaked wren of Andean cloud forest in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, often encountered in bamboo-dominated undergrowth and dense forest borders at 1,500–2,800 m. Its strongly streaked throat distinguishes it from most congeners. Pairs produce interlocking antiphonal duets that ring through the cloud forest.

children.name: Thryothorus
children.description: The largest wren genus in terms of species richness outside of Campylorhynchus reclassification, centred on the Americas. Carolina Wrens and their allies are noted for their powerful, musical songs and strong pair bonds maintained throughout the year.

children.name: Thryothorus ludovicianus
children.description: The Carolina wren is a species of wren common in the eastern United States, the extreme south of Ontario, Canada, the northeast and southeast of Mexico, and into northern Central America. Severe winters restrict the northern limits of their range, while favorable weather conditions lead to a northward extension of their breeding range. Their preferred habitat is in dense cover in forest, farm edges, and suburban areas.

children.name: Thryothorus nigricapillus
children.description: The bay wren (Cantorchilus nigricapillus) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Thryothorus galbraithii
children.description: Named after the British ornithologist John Galbraith, this Colombian endemic inhabits dense undergrowth in humid lowland forest on the Pacific slope of the western Andes. It is poorly known and rarely observed, with few modern records confirming its occurrence outside of the type locality. Its conservation status is considered near-threatened owing to ongoing deforestation.

children.name: Thryothorus semibadius
children.description: The riverside wren (Cantorchilus semibadius) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Thryothorus atricapilloides
children.description: The Pale-breasted Wren inhabits the arid coastal scrub, dry interior valleys, and thorn woodland of Peru, Ecuador, and extreme northern Chile. Its paler, buff-white underparts and less distinct facial markings distinguish it from the Buff-breasted Wren, which replaces it in more humid habitats to the north. It is among the most drought-tolerant wrens and can be found in some of the driest coastal desert scrub in South America.

children.name: Troglodytes
children.description: For their size, wrens produce one of the loudest songs of any bird — a rapid powerful torrent of trills carrying hundreds of metres through dense cover. In harsh Scandinavian winters dozens of wrens will huddle together in a nest box for warmth. One of Sweden's most widespread and numerous species despite its tiny size.

children.name: Troglodytes troglodytes
children.description: The Eurasian wren is a very small insectivorous bird and the only member of the wren family found in the Old World, specifically in Eurasia and Africa (Maghreb). In Anglophone Europe, it is commonly known simply as the wren. It has a very short tail which is often held erect, a short neck and a relatively long thin bill.

children.name: Troglodytes aedon
children.description: The northern house wren (Troglodytes aedon) is a very small passerine in the wren family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Troglodytes solstitialis
children.description: The mountain wren (Troglodytes solstitialis) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Troglodytes rufulus
children.description: The tepui wren (Troglodytes rufulus) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Troglodytes sissonii
children.description: The Socorro wren (Troglodytes sissonii) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Uropsila
children.description: A monotypic genus of small, round wrens of the forest understorey of Mexico and Central America, related to Henicorhina and sharing its skull-like creeping behaviour through dense tangles.

children.name: Henicorhina
children.description: The Wood-Wrens are small, almost tailless wrens of the Neotropical montane forest understorey, renowned for their extraordinarily powerful and melodious songs. Several recently described species occupy very narrow altitudinal and geographic ranges in the Andes.

children.name: Henicorhina darienensis
children.description: The Darien Wood-Wren was described in 2012 and is restricted to the cloud forests of the Darien region on the Colombia-Panama border. It had long been overlooked due to its superficial similarity to the Gray-breasted Wood-Wren but is now recognised as a distinct species based on song differences and genetic evidence. The Darien region's inaccessibility has contributed to the late discovery of this species.

children.name: Henicorhina bangsi
children.description: Named in honour of the American ornithologist Outram Bangs, this wood-wren is a Colombian endemic associated with the cloud forests of the Western and Central Andes. It has a very restricted distribution and is considered near-threatened due to extensive deforestation within its range. Recent molecular work supports its recognition as a species distinct from the Gray-breasted Wood-Wren.

children.name: Microcerculus
children.description: The nightingale-wrens are tiny, almost tailless wrens of the humid Neotropical forest floor, noted for their extraordinarily long, pure-toned songs. They creep through leaf litter and among roots on the forest floor in the manner of mice.

children.name: Microcerculus ustulatus
children.description: The flutist wren (Microcerculus ustulatus) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Cinnycerthia
children.description: The fulvous wrens are a group of large, richly coloured wrens of Andean cloud forests and high-elevation scrub. Closely related to the wood-wrens, they differ in their larger size and typically plain or lightly streaked rufous-brown plumage.

children.name: Cinnycerthia unirufa
children.description: The rufous wren (Cinnycerthia unirufa) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Cinnycerthia peruana
children.description: The Peruvian wren (Cinnycerthia peruana) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Cinnycerthia fulva
children.description: The fulvous wren (Cinnycerthia fulva) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Cinnycerthia cerverai
children.description: Named after the Spanish ornithologist Francisco Javier Cervera, the Sepia-brown Wren is the most recently described member of the genus, known from the cloud forests of northern Peru. It is distinguished from other Cinnycerthia by its darker, more uniformly sepia-brown plumage with less rufous tones. Its restricted range and specialised cloud forest habitat place it among Peru's most threatened passerines.

children.name: Odontorchilus
children.description: Two unusual wrens of the Neotropical forest canopy and sub-canopy, unique in the family for their predominantly arboreal, treetop-foraging habits. Both species are rarely encountered at lower levels.

children.name: Cyphorhinus
children.description: The song-wrens of the Neotropical forest floor and understorey, celebrated for producing some of the most hauntingly beautiful songs in the bird world. Their complex, organlike music has been compared to human choral singing.

children.name: Cyphorhinus aradus
children.description: The musician wren or organ wren (Cyphorhinus arada) is a species of wren named for its elaborate song.

children.name: Cyphorhinus modulator
children.description: The musician wren or organ wren (Cyphorhinus arada) is a species of wren named for its elaborate song.

children.name: Cyphorhinus phaeocephalus
children.description: The song wren (Cyphorhinus phaeocephalus) is a species of bird in the family Troglodytidae.

children.name: Donacobius
children.description: A monotypic genus of a strikingly patterned marsh bird of South America, sometimes placed in its own family Donacobiidae. The Black-capped Donacobius is unique in combining a wren-like body plan with social complexity and vocal duetting reminiscent of Old World babblers.

children.name: Bombycilla
children.description: Plump crested silky-plumaged birds named for the red wax-like tips on their secondary feathers. They breed in boreal Sweden's spruce-birch forest, subsisting on berries and insects. In winter they irrupt southward when the northern rowan crop fails — a waxwing invasion stripping Stockholm's ornamental rowans is one of the great Scandinavian winter spectacles.

children.name: Bombycilla garrulus
children.description: The Bohemian waxwing is a starling-sized passerine bird that breeds in the northern forests of the Palearctic and North America. It has mainly buff-grey plumage, black face markings and a pointed crest. Its wings are patterned with white and bright yellow, and some of the wing feathers have red tips, the resemblance of which to sealing wax gives these birds their common name.

children.name: Bombycilla cedrorum
children.description: The cedar waxwing (Bombycilla cedrorum) is a member of the family Bombycillidae or waxwing family of passerine birds.

children.name: Bombycilla japonica
children.description: The Japanese waxwing (Bombycilla japonica) is a fairly small passerine bird in the waxwing family found in the eastern Palaearctic, where it breeds south of the breeding range of the related Bohemian waxwing, but overlaps extensively with it in winter.

children.name: Emberiza
children.description: Seed-eating birds of open habitats. The Yellowhammer's lazy summer song is the defining sound of Swedish farmland hedgerows; it is now declining rapidly across Europe due to agricultural intensification. The Ortolan Bunting has collapsed in Sweden and is the subject of urgent conservation measures.

children.name: Emberiza citrinella
children.description: The yellowhammer is a passerine bird in the bunting family that is native to Eurasia and has been introduced to New Zealand and Australia. Most European birds remain in the breeding range year-round, but the eastern subspecies is partially migratory, with much of the population wintering further south. The male yellowhammer has a bright yellow head, streaked brown back, chestnut rump, and yellow under parts.

children.name: Emberiza schoeniclus
children.description: The common reed bunting, or simply reed bunting, is a passerine bird in the bunting family Emberizidae. This species breeds throughout Europe and much of the Palearctic region. While most individuals migrate south in winter, those in the milder south and west of the range are resident.

children.name: Emberiza hortulana
children.description: The ortolan, also called ortolan bunting, is a Eurasian bird in the bunting family Emberizidae, a passerine family now separated by most modern scholars from the finches, Fringillidae. The genus name Emberiza is from Alemannic German Embritz, a bunting. The specific name hortulana is from the Italian name for this bird, ortolana.

children.name: Emberiza pusilla
children.description: The little bunting is a passerine bird belonging to the bunting family (Emberizidae).

children.name: Emberiza calandra
children.description: The corn bunting is a passerine bird in the bunting family Emberizidae, a group now separated by most modern authors from the finches, Fringillidae. This is a large bunting with heavily streaked buff-brown plumage. The sexes are similar but the male is slightly larger than the female.

children.name: Emberiza cirlus
children.description: thumb| Emberiza cirlus - [[MHNT]] thumb| [[Cuculus canorus|Cuculus canorus canorus in a spawn of Emberiza cirlus - MHNT]].

children.name: Emberiza cia
children.description: The rock bunting (Emberiza cia) is a passerine bird in the bunting family Emberizidae, a group now separated by most modern authors from the finches, Fringillidae.

children.name: Emberiza rustica
children.description: The rustic bunting is a passerine bird in the bunting family Emberizidae, a group now separated by most modern authors from the finches, Fringillidae. The genus name Emberiza is from Old German Embritz, a bunting. The specific rustica is Latin for "rustic, simple".

children.name: Emberiza aureola
children.description: The yellow-breasted bunting is a passerine bird in the bunting family Emberizidae that is found across the Boreal and East Palearctic. The genus name Emberiza is from Old German Embritz, a bunting. The specific aureola is Latin for "golden".

children.name: Emberiza leucocephalos
children.description: The pine bunting (Emberiza leucocephalos) is a passerine bird in the bunting family Emberizidae, a group most modern authors now separate from the finches, Fringillidae.

children.name: Emberiza cioides
children.description: The meadow bunting or Siberian meadow bunting (Emberiza cioides) is a passerine bird of eastern Asia which belongs to the genus Emberiza in the bunting family Emberizidae.

children.name: Emberiza striolata
children.description: The striolated bunting (Emberiza striolata) is a passerine bird in the bunting family Emberizidae, a group now separated by most modern authors from the finches, Fringillidae.

children.name: Emberiza capensis
children.description: The Cape bunting (Emberiza capensis) is a passerine bird in the bunting family Emberizidae.

children.name: Emberiza sulphurata
children.description: :The name "yellow bunting" can also refer to the yellowhammer (Emberiza citrinella).

children.name: Emberiza variabilis
children.description: The grey bunting (Emberiza variabilis) is a species of bird in the family Emberizidae.

children.name: Emberiza koslowi
children.description: The Tibetan bunting (Emberiza koslowi) is a species of bird in the family Emberizidae.

children.name: Emberiza rutila
children.description: The chestnut bunting (Emberiza rutila) is a passerine bird in the bunting family Emberizidae found in the East Palearctic.

children.name: Emberiza siemsseni
children.description: The slaty bunting (Emberiza siemsseni) is a species of bird in the family Emberizidae.

children.name: Emberiza sahari
children.description: The house bunting (Emberiza sahari) is a passerine bird in the bunting family Emberizidae.

children.name: Emberiza poliopleura
children.description: The Somali bunting or Somali golden-breasted bunting (Emberiza poliopleura) is a species of bird in the family Emberizidae.

children.name: Emberiza socotrana
children.description: The Socotra bunting (Emberiza socotrana) is a species of bird in the family Emberizidae.

children.name: Emberiza lathami
children.description: The crested bunting (Emberiza lathami) is a species of bird in the family Emberizidae.

children.name: Plectrophenax
children.description: Hardy buntings of Arctic coasts and tundra, the males strikingly white in summer.

children.name: Plectrophenax nivalis
children.description: The snow bunting is a passerine bird in the family Calcariidae. It is an Arctic specialist, with a circumpolar Arctic breeding range throughout the northern hemisphere. There are small isolated populations on a few high mountain tops south of the Arctic region, including the Cairngorms in central Scotland and the Saint Elias Mountains on the southern Alaska-Yukon border, as well as the Cape Breton Highlands.

children.name: Calcarius
children.description: Ground-dwelling buntings of open tundra, the males with chestnut and black head patterns.

children.name: Calcarius lapponicus
children.description: The Lapland longspur, also known as the Lapland bunting, is a passerine bird in the longspur family Calcariidae. It is a circumpolar arctic breeder and the only member of the genus Calcarius present in Eurasia.

children.name: Rhynchophanes
children.description: A monotypic genus containing McCown's longspur of the North American shortgrass prairie. Formerly placed in Calcarius, it is now recognised as a distinct lineage on genetic grounds. Unlike other longspurs, it nests in loose colonies and performs spectacular aerial display flights.

children.name: Passer
children.description: Intimately associated with human settlement for thousands of years. The House Sparrow has declined catastrophically in western European cities since the 1990s, including Stockholm, probably due to loss of nest sites in modernised buildings and reduced invertebrate food for chicks. The Tree Sparrow is slightly more rural, identified by its chestnut crown and black ear spot.

children.name: Passer domesticus
children.description: The house sparrow is a bird of the sparrow family Passeridae, found in most parts of the world. It is a small bird that has a typical length of 16 cm (6.3 in) and a mass of 24–39.5 g (0.85–1.39 oz). Females and young birds are coloured pale brown and grey, and males have brighter black, white, and brown markings.

children.name: Passer montanus
children.description: The tree sparrow is a passerine bird in the sparrow family with a rich chestnut crown and nape and a black patch on each pure white cheek. The sexes have similar plumage, and young birds are duller versions of the adult. This sparrow breeds across much of temperate Eurasia and Southeast Asia and has been introduced elsewhere, including the United States, where it is known as the Eurasian tree sparrow or German sparrow to differentiate it from the native American tree sparrow.

children.name: Passer ammodendri
children.description: The saxaul sparrow (Passer ammodendri) is a passerine bird of the sparrow family (Passeridae), found in parts of Central Asia.

children.name: Passer castanopterus
children.description: The Somali sparrow (Passer castanopterus) is a species of bird in the family Passeridae found in Somalia, Djibouti, Ethiopia and Kenya.

children.name: Passer cordofanicus
children.description: The Kordofan sparrow (Passer cordofanicus), also known as the Kordofan rufous sparrow, is a sparrow found only in southwestern Sudan and adjacent border regions of South Sudan and Chad.

children.name: Passer eminibey
children.description: The chestnut sparrow (Passer eminibey) is a species of passerine bird in the sparrow family Passeridae.

children.name: Passer griseus
children.description: The northern grey-headed sparrow (Passer griseus), also known as the grey-headed sparrow, is a species of bird in the sparrow family Passeridae, which is resident in much of tropical Africa.

children.name: Passer hispaniolensis
children.description: The Spanish sparrow or willow sparrow (Passer hispaniolensis) is a passerine bird of the sparrow family Passeridae.

children.name: Passer iagoensis
children.description: The Iago sparrow (Passer iagoensis), also known as the Cape Verde or rufous-backed sparrow, is a passerine bird of the sparrow family Passeridae.

children.name: Passer insularis
children.description: The Socotra sparrow (Passer insularis) is a passerine bird endemic to the islands of Socotra, Samhah, and Darsah in the Indian Ocean, off the Horn of Africa.

children.name: Passer italiae
children.description: The Italian sparrow (Passer italiae), also known as the cisalpine sparrow, is a passerine bird of the sparrow family Passeridae, found in Italy and other parts of the Mediterranean region.

children.name: Passer melanurus
children.description: The Cape sparrow (Passer melanurus), or mossie, is a bird of the sparrow family Passeridae found in southern Africa.

children.name: Passer motitensis
children.description: The great sparrow (Passer motitensis), also known as the southern rufous sparrow, is found in southern Africa in dry, wooded savannah and towns.

children.name: Passer pyrrhonotus
children.description: The Sind sparrow (Passer pyrrhonotus) is a passerine bird of the sparrow family, Passeridae, found around the Indus valley region in South Asia.

children.name: Passer rufocinctus
children.description: The Kenya sparrow (Passer rufocinctus), also known as the Kenya rufous sparrow, is a sparrow found in Kenya and Tanzania.

children.name: Passer cinnamomeus
children.description: The russet sparrow (Passer cinnamomeus), also called the cinnamon or cinnamon tree sparrow, is a passerine bird of the sparrow family Passeridae.

children.name: Passer simplex
children.description: The desert sparrow (Passer simplex) is a species of bird in the sparrow family Passeridae, found in the Sahara Desert of northern Africa.

children.name: Passer suahelicus
children.description: The Swahili sparrow (Passer suahelicus) is a passerine bird of the sparrow family Passeridae.

children.name: Gymnoris
children.description: The bush sparrows or rock sparrows, a group of four Afrotropical and Asian species. They are medium-sized sparrows with relatively long tails and pale bills. Males typically have a yellow throat patch, especially conspicuous during the breeding season.

children.name: Petronia
children.description: The Rock Sparrow is the sole member of this genus, a sturdy, streaked bird of rocky hillsides and open stony terrain across southern Europe, North Africa, and Asia. It has a pale bill and a distinctive yellow patch on the breast that is often hard to see.

children.name: Petronia petronia
children.description: The rock sparrow or rock petronia (Petronia petronia) is a small passerine bird in the sparrow family Passeridae.

children.name: Carpospiza
children.description: The Pale Rockfinch is the only species in this genus, a pale, finch-like bird of arid rocky hillsides. It has a thin bill compared to other sparrows and a soft, lark-like song. It breeds from Turkey east to Afghanistan and winters in northeastern Africa.

children.name: Carpospiza brachydactyla
children.description: The pale rockfinch or pale rock sparrow (Carpospiza brachydactyla) is a small sparrow found in the Middle East and Central Asia.

children.name: Hypocryptadius
children.description: The Cinnamon Ibon is an enigmatic passerine endemic to the mountains of Mindanao in the Philippines. Long considered a white-eye, molecular studies have firmly placed it within Passeridae as the most basal sparrow lineage. It forages in forest canopies for insects and fruit.

children.name: Hypocryptadius cinnamomeus
children.description: The cinnamon ibon (Hypocryptadius cinnamomeus) is a species of bird endemic to the mountains of Mindanao in the Philippines.

children.name: Montifringilla
children.description: The snowfinches — sturdy, pale-bodied birds of high-altitude plateaus and mountain slopes. They are well-adapted to cold environments with extensive white in the wings and tail that is flashed in flight. They occur across the high mountains of southern Europe, Central Asia, and the Tibetan Plateau.

children.name: Montifringilla henrici
children.description: The Tibetan snowfinch or Henri's snowfinch (Montifringilla henrici) is a species of bird in the sparrow family.

children.name: Onychostruthus
children.description: The White-rumped Snowfinch is the sole species in this genus, distinguished from Montifringilla by its white rump and unique tail feather structure. It is a high-altitude specialist of the Tibetan Plateau, well-camouflaged against the rocky scree it inhabits.

children.name: Pyrgilauda
children.description: The ground snowfinches — four small, pale snowfinch species that inhabit the high-altitude steppes and rocky slopes of Central Asia and the Tibetan Plateau. They are more terrestrial than Montifringilla and have less white in the wings. Named after the Greek pyrgos (tower) and lauda (lark), reflecting their ground-dwelling habits.

children.name: Pyrgilauda theresae
children.description: The Afghan snowfinch (Pyrgilauda theresae) or the Afghan ground-sparrow, bar-tailed snowfinch, Meinertzhagen's snowfinch, or Theresa's snowfinch, is a passerine bird of the sparrow family Passeridae, endemic to the northern parts of the Hindu Kush mountains in Afghanistan.

children.name: Prunella
children.description: Unassuming mouse-like birds that shuffle through dense undergrowth. Despite superficial similarity to sparrows the thin insect-eating bill reveals their true nature. The Dunnock has one of the most complex mating systems of any European bird — males and females both pursue multiple partners simultaneously, leading to intense sperm competition and cooperative chick-rearing.

children.name: Prunella modularis
children.description: The dunnock is a small passerine, or perching bird, found throughout temperate Europe and into Asian Russia. Dunnocks have also been introduced and become common in New Zealand. It is the most widespread member of the accentor family; most other accentors are limited to mountain habitats.

children.name: Prunella collaris
children.description: The alpine accentor (Prunella collaris) is a small passerine bird in the family Prunellidae, which is native to Eurasia and North Africa.

children.name: Prunella montanella
children.description: The Siberian accentor (Prunella montanella) is a small passerine bird that breeds in northern Russia from the Ural Mountains eastwards across Siberia.

children.name: Prunella rubeculoides
children.description: thumb|Robin Accentor Male at Gnathang Valley, in East Sikkim, India The robin accentor (Prunella rubeculoides) is a species of bird in the family Prunellidae.

children.name: Prunella fulvescens
children.description: The brown accentor (Prunella fulvescens) is a species of bird in the family Prunellidae.

children.name: Prunella himalayana
children.description: The Altai accentor (Prunella himalayana) is a species of bird in the family Prunellidae.

children.name: Prunella rubida
children.description: The Japanese accentor (Prunella rubida) is a species of bird in the family Prunellidae.

children.name: Alauda
children.description: The Skylark's sustained spiralling song-flight — rising to a tiny dot 300 m above Swedish farmland — is one of the most celebrated sounds in northern European natural history. Populations have fallen by over half across Europe in 50 years due to changes in farming.

children.name: Alauda arvensis
children.description: The Eurasian skylark (Alauda arvensis), commonly referred to in Europe as the lark, is a passerine bird in the lark family, Alaudidae.

children.name: Alauda gulgula
children.description: The Oriental skylark (Alauda gulgula) is a species of skylark found in the Sino-Indian region and parts of central Asia.

children.name: Alauda razae
children.description: The Raso lark (Alauda razae) is a small passerine bird with a highly restricted range, being found only on Raso islet in the Cape Verde Islands.

children.name: Alauda japonica
children.description: The Japanese skylark (Alauda arvensis japonica) is a subspecies of the Eurasian skylark.

children.name: Lullula
children.description: A monotypic genus of sandy open country and heath, the Woodlark is distinguished from Alauda by its very short tail, prominent supercilia meeting at the bill, and a liquid, cascading song considered among the finest of any European passerine.

children.name: Lullula arborea
children.description: The woodlark or wood lark is the only extant species in the lark genus Lullula. It is found across most of Europe, the Middle East, western Asia and the mountains of north Africa. It is mainly resident (non-migratory) in the west of its range, but eastern populations of this passerine bird are more migratory, moving further south in winter.

children.name: Eremophila
children.description: Larks with striking black-and-yellow facial patterns and small feathered 'horns', breeding on open tundra, steppe, and desert plateaus across the Holarctic. The genus shows remarkable geographic variation, with dozens of subspecies adapted to different climatic zones.

children.name: Eremophila alpestris
children.description: The horned lark or shore lark is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae found across the northern hemisphere. It is known as "horned lark" in North America for distinctive feathers on the heads of the male birds in summer, and as "shore lark" in Europe because it can be found on shorelines in the winter.

children.name: Melanocorypha
children.description: Large, robust larks of open steppe and desert from the Iberian Peninsula east across Central Asia to Mongolia and China. Many species are partly or wholly migratory, and several are characterised by conspicuous white or black-tipped wing patterns visible in flight.

children.name: Melanocorypha calandra
children.description: The calandra lark (Melanocorypha calandra) or European calandra-lark breeds in warm temperate countries around the Mediterranean and eastwards through Turkey into northern Iran and southern Russia.

children.name: Melanocorypha bimaculata
children.description: The bimaculated lark (Melanocorypha bimaculata) breeds in warm temperate countries eastwards from Turkey into Central Asia.

children.name: Melanocorypha mongolica
children.description: The Mongolian lark (Melanocorypha mongolica) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae found from southern Russia and Mongolia to central China.

children.name: Melanocorypha yeltoniensis
children.description: The black lark (Melanocorypha yeltoniensis) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae found in south-eastern Russia and Kazakhstan.

children.name: Melanocorypha maxima
children.description: The Tibetan lark (Melanocorypha maxima) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae found on the Tibetan Plateau from north-western India to central China.

children.name: Calandrella
children.description: Small, compact short-toed larks of arid and semi-arid open country across the Palearctic, Middle East, and East Africa. The genus includes several cryptic species, best separated by voice, range, and subtle structural features.

children.name: Calandrella brachydactyla
children.description: The greater short-toed lark (Calandrella brachydactyla) is a small passerine bird.

children.name: Calandrella rufescens
children.description: thumb|Eggs of Alaudala rufescens minor [[MHNT]].

children.name: Calendulauda
children.description: African bush-larks and related savanna and scrubland species, largely confined to sub-Saharan Africa and the southern half of the continent. Many members are skulking birds of dense vegetation, detected more easily by song than by sight.

children.name: Calendulauda albescens
children.description: The Karoo lark (Calendulauda albescens) or red-backed lark is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae.

children.name: Calendulauda burra
children.description: The red lark (Calendulauda burra), also known as the ferruginous lark or ferruginous sand-lark, is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae.

children.name: Calendulauda erythrochlamys
children.description: The dune lark (Calendulauda erythrochlamys) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae.

children.name: Calendulauda sabota
children.description: The sabota lark (Calendulauda sabota) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae.

children.name: Calendulauda seebohmi
children.description: Barlow's Lark is a recently recognised species of coastal Namibia, separated from the Karoo Lark on the basis of plumage, song, and habitat differences. It inhabits dry, stony scrub on gravel plains close to the Atlantic coast.

children.name: Eremalauda
children.description: Small desert larks of sandy and stony wastes in North Africa, the Sahara-Sahel zone, and the Arabian Peninsula. Often pale and cryptically coloured, they are adapted to extreme aridity with a preference for sparse, wind-rippled sand surfaces.

children.name: Spizocorys
children.description: Small, short-billed larks of dry grassland, steppe, and semi-arid scrub in Africa, characterised by compact build and often heavily streaked plumage. Several species are Near Threatened or restricted to the Horn of Africa.

children.name: Spizocorys obbiensis
children.description: The Obbia lark (Spizocorys obbiensis) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae.

children.name: Spizocorys personata
children.description: The masked lark (Spizocorys personata) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae.

children.name: Galerida
children.description: Crested larks with prominent, always-erect crests, widespread from Western Europe and North Africa across the Middle East and South Asia to Southeast Asia. They favour open, often disturbed habitats including roadsides, cultivation margins, and semi-desert, and are largely sedentary.

children.name: Galerida cristata
children.description: The crested lark (Galerida cristata) is a species of lark widespread across Eurasia and northern Africa.

children.name: Galerida malabarica
children.description: The Malabar lark, or Malabar crested lark (Galerida malabarica) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae found in western India.

children.name: Galerida modesta
children.description: The sun lark (Galerida modesta) or Nigerian sun lark, is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae.

children.name: Mirafra
children.description: The largest genus of larks, comprising African and Asian bush-larks of open woodland, savanna, and grassland. Many Mirafra larks are best identified by their wing-snapping display flights and elaborate, musical songs; plumage is often cryptically variable.

children.name: Mirafra angolensis
children.description: The Angola lark (Amirafra angolensis) or Angola bushlark is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae found in southern and central Africa.

children.name: Mirafra ashi
children.description: The Somali lark (Corypha somalica) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae endemic to Somalia.

children.name: Mirafra cheniana
children.description: The melodious lark (Mirafra cheniana) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae found in southern Africa.

children.name: Mirafra cordofanica
children.description: Kordofan lark (Mirafra cordofanica) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae found in Africa.

children.name: Mirafra somalica
children.description: The Somali lark (Corypha somalica) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae endemic to Somalia.

children.name: Mirafra rufocinnamomea
children.description: The flappet lark (Amirafra rufocinnamomea) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae that is widespread across Sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Mirafra hova
children.description: The Madagascar lark (Eremopterix hova) is a species of lark in the family Alaudidae endemic to Madagascar.

children.name: Mirafra passerina
