children.name: Lagonosticta virata
children.description: The Mali firefinch (Lagonosticta virata) is a species of estrildid finch found in Western Africa.

children.name: Lagonosticta sanguinodorsalis
children.description: The rock firefinch (Lagonosticta sanguinodorsalis) is a species of estrildid finch found in the Jos Plateau of central Nigeria and in Cameroon.

children.name: Lagonosticta umbrinodorsalis
children.description: The Chad firefinch or Reichenow's firefinch (Lagonosticta umbrinodorsalis) is a small passerine bird belonging to the firefinch genus Lagonosticta in the estrildid finch family Estrildidae.

children.name: Granatina
children.description: A small genus of spectacular African estrildids noted for their brilliant violet, blue, and chestnut plumage. The Violet-eared Waxbill and Purple Grenadier are among the most beautiful of all African finches, with males displaying an extraordinary array of iridescent colours. They inhabit dry savanna and thorn scrub.

children.name: Granatina ianthinogaster
children.description: The purple grenadier (Granatina ianthinogaster) is a common species of estrildid finch found in eastern Africa.

children.name: Coccopygia
children.description: A small genus of African waxbills with yellow or greenish underparts and distinctive red rumps. They are among the smallest estrildids, with delicate bills and active, acrobatic feeding habits. They inhabit montane grasslands, forest edges, and cultivated areas in eastern and southern Africa.

children.name: Coccopygia melanotis
children.description: The swee waxbill (Coccopygia melanotis), is a common species of estrildid finch native to Southern Africa.

children.name: Pyrenestes
children.description: The seedcrackers — a small genus of African estrildids with massively thick, powerful bills adapted for cracking the hardest seeds. They exhibit a remarkable polymorphism in bill size, with two distinct morphs occurring within the same population. They inhabit forests and dense thickets.

children.name: Pyrenestes sanguineus
children.description: The crimson seedcracker (Pyrenestes sanguineus) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa.

children.name: Pyrenestes minor
children.description: The lesser seedcracker or Nyasa seedcracker (Pyrenestes minor) is a fairly common species of estrildid finch found in eastern Africa.

children.name: Pytilia
children.description: The pytilias — a genus of colourful African estrildids with green or red wings and finely barred underparts. They are active, often confiding birds of savanna and woodland edges. Their flight is fast and direct with a characteristic whirring sound.

children.name: Cryptospiza
children.description: The crimson-wings — a small genus of shy, forest-dwelling African estrildids with red wings, olive-green bodies, and dark faces. They are secretive birds of montane forest undergrowth, often difficult to observe as they forage quietly in deep shade.

children.name: Cryptospiza jacksoni
children.description: The dusky crimsonwing (Cryptospiza jacksoni) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Africa.

children.name: Cryptospiza salvadorii
children.description: The Abyssinian crimsonwing (Cryptospiza salvadorii), also known as the Ethiopian crimsonwing, Salvadori's crimsonwing or crimson-backed forest finch, is a common species of estrildid finch found in eastern Africa.

children.name: Hypargos
children.description: The twinspots — a small genus of beautifully patterned African estrildids with spotted breasts and bright rumps. They are shy, retiring birds of forest undergrowth and dense thickets, often more easily heard than seen. Their melodious calls are characteristic sounds of African forests.

children.name: Euschistospiza
children.description: A small genus of African estrildids related to the twinspots, with finely spotted breasts and rich maroon or dusky plumage. They are shy, secretive birds of montane and lowland forests, foraging on the ground in dense cover.

children.name: Euschistospiza cinereovinacea
children.description: The dusky twinspot (Euschistospiza cinereovinacea) is a species of estrildid finch found in Sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Nigrita
children.description: The negrofinches — a genus of African estrildids with contrasting black, grey, and white plumage, found in forests and woodlands across sub-Saharan Africa. They are active, acrobatic birds that forage in the canopy and understory, often in mixed-species flocks.

children.name: Nesocharis
children.description: The olivebacks — a small genus of African estrildids with olive-green and grey plumage, thick bills, and a distinctive white collar. They are found in forests and montane scrub of West and Central Africa, where they forage quietly in the canopy for seeds and small fruits.

children.name: Parmoptila
children.description: The antpeckers — a small genus of African estrildids with finely spotted plumage and a unique association with ants. They are named for their habit of following ant columns to feed on insects flushed by the ants, a behaviour unusual among estrildids. They have stout, rather finch-like bills.

children.name: Paludipasser
children.description: A monotypic genus of African estrildid containing the Locust Finch, a small, secretive bird of wetlands and moist grasslands. It is named for its preference for grasshopper and locust nymphs, which supplement its seed-based diet. It is one of the most elusive of the African waxbills.

children.name: Paludipasser locustellus
children.description: A tiny finch with brown upperparts, a red face and rump, and pale underparts. It is found in moist grasslands and marshes of Central and East Africa, often near water.

children.name: Ortygospiza
children.description: The quailfinches — a small genus of terrestrial estrildids resembling miniature quail in their shape and ground-dwelling habits. They are found in moist grasslands and marshes across Africa, where they forage on the ground for grass seeds. Their short, rounded wings and strong legs reflect their largely terrestrial lifestyle.

children.name: Ortygospiza fuscocrissa
children.description: The African quailfinch, spectacled quailfinch, or white-chinned quailfinch (Ortygospiza atricollis fuscocrissa), is a common species of estrildid finch found in eastern and southern Africa.

children.name: Amurestes
children.description: A genus of African estrildids with distinctive black, red, and white plumage patterns. The Crimson Seedcracker and related species have massively developed bills for cracking hard seeds.

children.name: Amurestes obscurus
children.description: A finch with a red face, dark brown upperparts, and grey underparts. It is found in forests of Central Africa.

children.name: Sporaeginthus
children.description: A small genus of African estrildids known as the seedeaters or cordon-bleus, with bright blue plumage on the face and underparts. They are among the most beautiful of the small African finches.

children.name: Emblema
children.description: A monotypic genus of Australian estrildid containing the Painted Finch, a strikingly coloured bird of rocky hillsides and arid scrublands. It is named for its brilliant red and black facial pattern that resembles painted markings.

children.name: Emblema pictum
children.description: The painted finch (Emblema pictum) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Australia.

children.name: Stagonopleura
children.description: The firetails — a genus of Australian estrildids with brilliant crimson rumps and tails, found in coastal and forested regions of Australia. They are plump, active finches with distinctive black-and-white patterns on the face and throat.

children.name: Stagonopleura guttata
children.description: The diamond firetail (Stagonopleura guttata) is a species of estrildid finch that is endemic to Australia.

children.name: Stagonopleura bella
children.description: The beautiful firetail (Stagonopleura bella) is a common species of estrildid finch found in Australia.

children.name: Neochmia
children.description: A genus of Australian estrildids with brilliant red markings on the face and rump, found in grasslands and woodlands across Australia. They are lively, active finches that often gather in large flocks.

children.name: Neochmia ruficauda
children.description: The star finch (Emblema ruficauda) is a seed-eating bird species found in northern Australia.

children.name: Poephila
children.description: The grassfinches — a genus of long-tailed Australian estrildids with black bibs and chestnut or grey plumage. They are birds of arid and semi-arid grasslands, often seen in large flocks drinking at waterholes.

children.name: Poephila personata
children.description: The masked finch (Poephila personata) is a small passerine bird in the estrildid finch family, Estrildidae.

children.name: Heteromunia
children.description: A monotypic genus of Australian estrildid containing the Pictorella Munia, a distinctive finch with a scaly white breast and a blue-grey bill. It is found in dry grasslands of northern Australia.

children.name: Heteromunia pectoralis
children.description: The pictorella mannikin, pictorella munia, or pictorella finch (Heteromunia pectoralis) is small brown and grey finch with a grey bill and distinctive scaly white breast plate which is endemic to northern Australia.

children.name: Odontospiza
children.description: A monotypic genus of African estrildid containing the Crimson-rumped Waxbill, a small finch with a bright red rump and distinctive facial markings. It is found in dry savannas of East Africa.

children.name: Glaucopectus
children.description: A genus of African estrildids with distinctive blue-grey bills and finely patterned plumage, found in savannas and woodlands of Africa.

children.name: Glaucopectus angolensis
children.description: A small waxbill with a blue-grey bill, brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a red rump. It is found in savannas of southwestern Africa.

children.name: Estrildopas
children.description: A small genus of African estrildids with black, white, and rufous plumage patterns, found in forests of Central Africa.

children.name: Estrildopas ruficeps
children.description: A waxbill with a rufous crown, black face, olive upperparts, and pale underparts. It is found in lowland forests of Central Africa.

children.name: Madagascara
children.description: A genus of estrildids endemic to Madagascar, with olive, yellow, and red plumage. They inhabit forests and scrub across the island.

children.name: Madagascara madagascariensis
children.description: A small finch with brown upperparts, white underparts, and a black face and throat. It is endemic to Madagascar, inhabiting grasslands and forests.

children.name: Madagascara nana
children.description: A tiny finch with brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a short tail. It is endemic to Madagascar, inhabiting grasslands and wetlands.

children.name: Carpophaga
children.description: A genus of Pacific island estrildids with thick bills and brown, black, and white plumage. They are found on islands of the southwest Pacific.

children.name: Carpophaga melanura
children.description: A stocky munia with a black tail, brown upperparts, white underparts, and a thick grey bill. It is found on islands of Fiji and Tonga.

children.name: Carpophaga pectoralis
children.description: A munia with a white breast, brown upperparts, black belly, and thick bill. It is found on islands of Vanuatu and New Caledonia.

children.name: Leucosticte
children.description: A genus of mountain-dwelling finches with grey, brown, and pink plumage, found in high-altitude regions of Asia and North America. They are adapted to the harshest environments on Earth.

children.name: Calliphthalmus
children.description: A genus of African estrildids with bright red or orange bills and colourful plumage, found in savannas and woodlands.

children.name: Calliphthalmus erythrothorax
children.description: A waxbill with a red breast, brown upperparts, and a red bill. It is found in savannas of West Africa.

children.name: Calliphthalmus rubriventris
children.description: A waxbill with a red belly, brown upperparts, and a red bill. It is found in savannas of central Africa.

children.name: Calliphthalmus flaviventris
children.description: A waxbill with a yellow belly, brown upperparts, and a red bill. It is found in savannas of southern Africa.

children.name: Calliphthalmus nigrimentum
children.description: A waxbill with a black chin, brown upperparts, and pale underparts. It is found in savannas of East Africa.

children.name: Entomophaga
children.description: A genus of insectivorous estrildids found in the forests of Central Africa, with olive and yellow plumage and fine bills adapted for catching small insects.

children.name: Entomophaga insectivora
children.description: A small waxbill with olive upperparts, yellow underparts, and a fine black bill. It is found in lowland forests of central Africa.

children.name: Entomophaga chloropoda
children.description: A waxbill with green legs, olive upperparts, and yellow underparts. It is found in montane forests of East Africa.

children.name: Entomophaga flaviventris
children.description: A small finch with bright yellow underparts, olive upperparts, and a thin bill. It is found in forests of central Africa.

children.name: Agelaius
children.description: The red-winged and yellow-winged blackbirds — medium-sized icterids named for their distinctive shoulder patches. Males are black with bold red or yellow epaulets, which they flash aggressively during territorial displays. They are highly polygynous, with dominant males defending territories that attract multiple females, who build nests woven into cattails and marsh vegetation.

children.name: Agelaius tricolor
children.description: The tricolored blackbird (Agelaius tricolor) is a passerine bird of the family Icteridae.

children.name: Quiscalus
children.description: The grackles — large, glossy blackbirds with long, keeled tails and pale yellow eyes. They are among the most intelligent of all songbirds, capable of solving complex puzzles and remembering individual human faces. Grackles are highly social, forming enormous noisy roosts, and have adapted brilliantly to urban and suburban environments.

children.name: Quiscalus quiscula
children.description: The common grackle (Quiscalus quiscula) is an icterid bird found in large numbers through much of North America.

children.name: Quiscalus nicaraguensis
children.description: The Nicaraguan grackle (Quiscalus nicaraguensis) is a species of passerine bird belonging to the genus Quiscalus, a genus of grackles in the New World blackbird family, Icteridae.

children.name: Quiscalus lugubris
children.description: The Carib grackle (Quiscalus lugubris) is a New World tropical blackbird, a resident breeder in the Lesser Antilles and northern South America east of the Andes, from Colombia east to Venezuela and northeastern Brazil.

children.name: Molothrus
children.description: The cowbirds — obligate brood parasites that lay their eggs in the nests of other passerine species. They are named for their historical association with bison herds, following the great herds to feed on insects flushed by their movement. A single female may lay several dozen eggs in a season, each in a different host nest, never building a nest or rearing her own young.

children.name: Molothrus bonariensis
children.description: The shiny cowbird (Molothrus bonariensis) is a passerine bird in the New World family Icteridae.

children.name: Molothrus rufoaxillaris
children.description: The screaming cowbird (Molothrus rufoaxillaris) is an obligate brood parasite belonging to the family Icteridae and is found in South America.

children.name: Molothrus oryzivorus
children.description: The giant cowbird (Molothrus oryzivorus) is a large passerine bird in the New World family Icteridae.

children.name: Molothrus aeneus
children.description: The bronzed cowbird (Molothrus aeneus), also known as the red-eyed cowbird, is a small icterid native to North America.

children.name: Icterus
children.description: The New World orioles — brilliantly coloured blackbirds with a striking contrast of black and bright yellow, orange, or chestnut. They build remarkable hanging pouch nests woven from plant fibres, suspended from branch tips. Males sing rich, fluty whistles that carry through the treetops. They are primarily frugivorous and insectivorous, and many species undertake long migrations between breeding and wintering grounds.

children.name: Icterus galbula
children.description: The Baltimore oriole (Icterus galbula) is a small icterid blackbird common in eastern North America as a migratory breeding bird.

children.name: Icterus spurius
children.description: The orchard oriole (Icterus spurius) is the smallest species of icterid.

children.name: Icterus cayanensis
children.description: | range_map = Icterus cayanensis map 3.svg.

children.name: Icterus cucullatus
children.description: The hooded oriole (Icterus cucullatus) is a medium-sized New World oriole.

children.name: Icterus gularis
children.description: The Altamira oriole (Icterus gularis) is a New World oriole.

children.name: Icterus icterus
children.description: The Venezuelan troupial, known in Venezuela as the Turpial (Icterus icterus), is the national bird of Venezuela.

children.name: Icterus jamacaii
children.description: The campo troupial or campo oriole (Icterus jamacaii) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae that is found in northeastern Brazil.

children.name: Icterus bonana
children.description: The Martinique oriole (Icterus bonana) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Icterus oberi
children.description: The Montserrat oriole (Icterus oberi) is a medium-sized black-and-yellow icterid (the same family as many blackbirds, meadowlarks, cowbirds, grackles, and others, including the New World orioles).

children.name: Icterus fuertesi
children.description: The orchard oriole (Icterus spurius) is the smallest species of icterid.

children.name: Icterus auratus
children.description: The orange oriole (Icterus auratus) is a small bird species with orange feathers native to the Icteridae family in the Yucatán Peninsula.

children.name: Xanthocephalus
children.description: The yellow-headed blackbird — a striking monotypic genus named for the male's vivid yellow head and breast. It breeds in the marshes of western and central North America, often alongside Red-winged Blackbirds. Males defend territories in deep-water cattail marshes and perform impressive flight displays, singing a grating, strained song while hanging from cattail stems.

children.name: Dolichonyx
children.description: The bobolink — a monotypic genus of Grassland icterid with one of the longest migrations of any passerine. The male's breeding plumage is unique among North American birds: black below and on the head, with a buff nape and white back and rump. The species is named for its bubbling, ecstatic song, which pours forth in sustained, tumbling phrases from the male's flight display over hayfields and prairies.

children.name: Sturnella
children.description: The meadowlarks — stocky, ground-dwelling icterids with bright yellow underparts and a bold black V on the breast. Despite their name they are not larks but true blackbirds, and are among the most iconic birds of American grasslands. Their clear, fluting songs carry across open fields, and they are more often heard than seen, perching on fence posts and low trees to deliver their melodies.

children.name: Sturnella magna
children.description: The eastern meadowlark (Sturnella magna) is a medium-sized icterid bird, very similar in appearance to its sister species, the western meadowlark.

children.name: Sturnella neglecta
children.description: The western meadowlark (Sturnella neglecta) is a medium-sized icterid bird, about in length.

children.name: Leistes
children.description: A genus of South American meadowlarks separated from Sturnella by genetic evidence, with bright red or yellow underparts and a strong preference for grasslands. Males are highly territorial and perform conspicuous flight displays.

children.name: Leistes bellicosus
children.description: The Peruvian meadowlark (Leistes bellicosus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae, the oropendolas, New World orioles, and New World blackbirds.

children.name: Leistes defilippii
children.description: The Pampas meadowlark (Leistes defilippii) is a Vulnerable species of bird in the family Icteridae, the oropendolas, New World orioles, and New World blackbirds.

children.name: Euphagus
children.description: The American blackbirds — a small genus of two species that bridge the gap between grackles and true blackbirds. They are medium-sized icterids with glossy black plumage, pale eyes, and relatively slender bills. One species is a common bird of towns and farms, while the other has suffered a dramatic and poorly understood population decline.

children.name: Euphagus carolinus
children.description: The rusty blackbird (Euphagus carolinus) is a medium-sized New World blackbird, closely related to grackles ("rusty grackle" is an older name for the species).

children.name: Cacicus
children.description: The caciques — medium-sized icterids with predominantly black plumage accented by bright yellow, red, or orange patches. They are social birds that build long, hanging pouch nests in colonies, often near wasp nests for protection from predators.

children.name: Cacicus solitarius
children.description: The solitary cacique or solitary black cacique (Cacicus solitarius) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Cacicus koepckeae
children.description: The Selva cacique (Cacicus koepckeae) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Cacicus sclateri
children.description: The Ecuadorian cacique (Cacicus sclateri) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Cacicus chrysonotus
children.description: The mountain cacique (Cacicus chrysonotus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Psarocolius
children.description: The oropendolas — large icterids with striking combination of black, chestnut, and yellow plumage, and long, pointed bills with colourful tips. They are colonial breeders that weave extraordinary hanging nests up to two metres long, suspended from isolated trees.

children.name: Psarocolius viridis
children.description: The green oropendola (Psarocolius viridis) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Psarocolius bifasciatus
children.description: The olive oropendola (Psarocolius bifasciatus) is the largest member of the icterid family and rivals the Amazonian umbrellabird as the largest passerine bird in South America.

children.name: Psarocolius montezuma
children.description: The Montezuma oropendola (Psarocolius montezuma) is a New World tropical icterid bird.

children.name: Psarocolius guatimozinus
children.description: The black oropendola (Psarocolius guatimozinus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae (New World blackbirds).

children.name: Gymnomystax
children.description: The oriole blackbird — a monotypic genus of striking black-and-yellow icterid found in South America. Despite its name, it is not a true oriole but a blackbird with a similar colour pattern.

children.name: Gymnomystax mexicanus
children.description: The oriole blackbird (Gymnomystax mexicanus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Dives
children.description: A genus of medium-sized, entirely black icterids with a strong, musical song and a preference for open habitats. They are the most thrush-like in appearance among the blackbirds.

children.name: Dives dives
children.description: The melodious blackbird (Dives dives) is a New World tropical bird.

children.name: Dives warczewiczi
children.description: The scrub blackbird (Dives warczewiczi) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Curaeus curaeus
children.description: thumb|Molothrus bonariensis in a clutch of Curaeus curaeus - [[MHNT]].

children.name: Nesopsar nigerrimus
children.description: The Jamaican blackbird (Nesopsar nigerrimus) is a species of bird in the New World blackbird and oriole family Icteridae.

children.name: Gnorimopsar chopi
children.description: The chopi blackbird (Gnorimopsar chopi) is a species of passerine bird belonging to the family Icteridae, which contains the New World blackbirds, grackles, New World orioles and related species.

children.name: Oreopsar bolivianus
children.description: | range_map = Agelaioides oreopsar map.svg.

children.name: Agelaioides badius
children.description: The grayish baywing (Agelaioides badius), formerly known as the bay-winged cowbird, is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Cercomochus
children.description: Cercomochus — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Cercomochus nebulosus
children.description: A small, elusive bird with a strikingly patterned plumage. Found in dense forests and wetlands, it has become difficult to study due to its cryptic nature.

children.name: Chrysotheretia
children.description: Chrysotheretia — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Chrysotheretia garrula
children.description: A vibrant bird with a distinctive yellow throat and black streaks on its breast. They are known for their melodious song, which can be heard throughout the summer.

children.name: Piranga luteola
children.description: A striking bird with a bright yellow throat and upperparts, this species is found in riparian areas and wetlands. Its cheerful song adds to the chorus of spring.

children.name: Halcyon fulva
children.description: This bird is known for its bright yellow throat and upperparts. It is a specialized feeder, often seen in riparian areas.

children.name: Daphoenus
children.description: Daphoenus — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Daphoenus obscurus
children.description: This tiny bird is a specialist feeder, spending much of its time probing into the leaf litter for insect prey. It has a unique call that can be heard throughout the forest understory.

children.name: Chrysolophus leucophrys
children.description: This unique bird is named for its distinctive song and feeding habits. It is a specialized feeder, often seen flying over wetlands in search of insects.

children.name: Ambrosiceps cassinii
children.description: A small, olive-green bird with a distinctive white eye ring and prominent yellow bill. Found in coastal scrub and wetlands from Nova Scotia to Texas.

children.name: Chlorospingus flavescens
children.description: A small, olive-green bird with a yellow wash on the underparts and distinctive white eye ring. Found in open woodlands from New Mexico to Florida.

children.name: Eurymachus
children.description: Eurymachus — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Eurymachus eximius
children.description: This warbler has a unique habitat preference, being found only in the cavities of hollow trees. Its striking plumage and song are characteristic features of this species.

children.name: Leptopumachus
children.description: Leptopumachus — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Leptopumachus lepidus
children.description: Known for its iridescent feathers and melodious song, this species is found in the southern regions of North America. Its bright plumage makes it easily recognizable.

children.name: Terekeca ciliata
children.description: This warbler is known for its crested head and striking plumage. It can often be found in the canopy of mature forests, where it feeds on insects.

children.name: Euphronia canorus
children.description: This bird is known for its distinctive call and overall patterned plumage. It is a specialized feeder, often seen in wetlands.

children.name: Melozone
children.description: Melozone — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Melozone maculatus
children.description: This waterthrush is named for its spotted plumage. It is a secretive bird, often only glimpsed by those who listen carefully to the sounds of running streams and water.

children.name: Polioptila
children.description: Polioptila — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Polioptila rufa
children.description: This small warbler is named for its striking black and white plumage. It is a secretive feeder, often seen in dense foliage. Its vocalizations are characteristic of the eastern forests.

children.name: Certhia
children.description: Certhia — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Certhia melanocephala
children.description: This bird is distinguished by its striking black cap and overall brown plumage. It is a specialized feeder, often seen in coniferous forests.

children.name: Cardinalis
children.description: The true cardinals — crested, thick-billed passerines named for the brilliant red plumage of the male, which resembles the robes of Catholic cardinals. They are among the most recognisable and popular birds in the Americas, with a rich vocabulary of whistled songs.

children.name: Cardinalis cardinalis
children.description: The northern cardinal (Cardinalis cardinalis), also commonly known as the common cardinal, red cardinal, or simply cardinal, is a bird in the genus Cardinalis.

children.name: Cardinalis phoeniceus
children.description: The vermilion cardinal (Cardinalis phoeniceus) is a species of bird in the family Cardinalidae, the cardinals or cardinal grosbeaks.

children.name: Pseudocyanocompsa viridis
children.description: The Green-crowned Quail is a medium-sized bird with a distinctive green crown and white throat patch. Found in shrublands and woodland edges, it feeds on seeds and fruits. Males have a bright red breast.

children.name: Granatellus caerulescens
children.description: The Blue-throated Granate is a small bird with a bright blue throat patch and reddish-brown plumage. It inhabits open savannas and grasslands, where it feeds on insects and seeds. Males sing complex songs during breeding.

children.name: Pheucticus
children.description: New World grosbeaks with massive conical bills adapted for cracking hard seeds and nuts. Males are boldly patterned in black, white, and bright yellow or rose-red.

children.name: Pheucticus chrysogaster
children.description: The golden grosbeak (Pheucticus chrysogaster), also known as golden-bellied grosbeak or southern yellow grosbeak, is a species of grosbeak in the family Cardinalidae.

children.name: Pheucticus chrysopeplus
children.description: The yellow grosbeak (Pheucticus chrysopeplus), also known as the Mexican yellow grosbeak, is a medium-sized seed-eating bird in the same family as the northern cardinal, "tropical" or "New World" buntings, and "cardinal-grosbeaks" or New World grosbeaks.

children.name: Passerina
children.description: New World buntings — small, brilliantly coloured seed-eating birds with vivid blues, indigos, and greens in the males. Young males take two years to attain full adult plumage.

children.name: Passerina caerulea
children.description: The blue grosbeak (Passerina caerulea) is a medium-sized North American passerine bird in the cardinal family Cardinalidae.

children.name: Cyanocompsa brissonii

children.name: Amaurospiza

children.name: Amaurospiza concolor

children.name: Chlorothraupis monticola
children.description: The Mountain Emerald is a small bird with bright green plumage and white throat patch. It inhabits mountain forests and shrublands, where it feeds on insects and seeds. Males sing complex songs during breeding.

children.name: Piranga

children.name: Granatellus

children.name: Cyanoloxia rothschildii

children.name: Setophaga
children.description: The typical wood-warblers — a large and diverse genus of small, insectivorous passerines that forms the core of the Parulidae. Males in breeding plumage display bold patterns of yellow, black, white, blue, and chestnut; females and non-breeding birds are more subdued. They are among the most sought-after birds by North American birders during spring migration, when males sing from treetops in brilliant breeding colours.

children.name: Setophaga vitellina

children.name: Setophaga pitiayumi

children.name: Setophaga batesii

children.name: Geothlypis flavida
children.description: A small, greenish warbler with a bright yellow throat and breast. Known for its loud, high-pitched calls during the breeding season, this species is found in deciduous forests and woodlands.

children.name: Protonotaria grisea
children.description: A small, olive-brown warbler with a strikingly white throat and underparts. Known for its distinctive hooting song, this species is found in wooded swamps and wetlands of the southeastern United States.

children.name: Seiurus ohiensis
children.description: A small, brown warbler with a distinctive white band across the breast and yellow flanks. Known for its steady hopping on the ground in search of insect prey, this species is found along streams and rivers in eastern North America.

children.name: Mniotilta vellei
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a bright white throat and breast. Known for its loud, raspy calls during the breeding season, this species is found in forests along the Atlantic coast.

children.name: Parkesia albifrons
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a yellow breast and belly. Known for its distinctive call that sounds like the bark of an old oak tree, this species is found in deciduous forests.

children.name: Cardellina leucophrys
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a bright white throat and breast. Known for its loud, buzzy song during the breeding season, this species is found in coastal wetlands.

children.name: Leiothlypis brevicauda
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a white eyebrow and breast. Known for its high-pitched trills during the breeding season, this species is found in open woodlands.

children.name: Oporornis dominica
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a white throat and breast. Known for its loud, whistling song during the breeding season, this species is found in coastal forests.

children.name: Vermivora cinerea
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a black throat and breast. Known for its distinctive call that sounds like “cheer cheer,” this species is found in deciduous forests.

children.name: Myioborus lucernarius
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a white throat and breast. Known for its melodious song during the breeding season, this species is found in coastal forests of South America.

children.name: Basileuterus rufogularis
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a rufous throat and breast. Known for its distinctive call that sounds like “chip chip,” this species is found in tropical forests.

children.name: Myiothlypis fulvogularis
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a yellow throat and breast. Known for its melodious song during the breeding season, this species is found in coastal forests of South America.

children.name: Oreothlypis nigriceps
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a black throat and breast. Known for its loud, raspy calls during the breeding season, this species is found in coastal forests.

children.name: Geothlypis
children.description: The yellowthroats — a genus of stocky, skulking warblers of dense, wet vegetation. Males are distinguished by a bold black mask across the face, bordered above by a white or grey band. They are more often heard than seen, delivering a loud, repetitive 'wichity-wichity-wichity' song from the depths of cattail marshes and brushy swamps.

children.name: Geothlypis trichas
children.description: The common yellowthroat (Geothlypis trichas) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Geothlypis formosa
children.description: The Kentucky warbler (Geothlypis formosa) is a small species of New World warbler.

children.name: Geothlypis philadelphia
children.description: The mourning warbler (Geothlypis philadelphia) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.

children.name: Geothlypis flavovelata
children.description: The Altamira yellowthroat (Geothlypis flavovelata) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Geothlypis rostrata
children.description: The Bahama yellowthroat (Geothlypis rostrata) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Geothlypis aequinoctialis
children.description: The masked yellowthroat (Geothlypis aequinoctialis) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Protonotaria
children.description: The prothonotary warbler — a monotypic genus of cavity-nesting warbler named for the golden-yellow robes of papal notaries. It is one of only two Parulidae species that nest in tree cavities, and the only eastern North American warbler to do so. Its brilliant colouration and gentle song make it one of the most prized species among birders.

children.name: Protonotaria citrea
children.description: The prothonotary warbler (Protonotaria citrea) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.

children.name: Seiurus
children.description: The ovenbird — a monotypic genus of large, terrestrial warbler named for its distinctive domed nest, which resembles a dutch oven. It is one of the few warblers that forages entirely on the forest floor, walking deliberately in search of invertebrates. Its loud, ringing 'teacher-TEACHER-TEACHER' song is one of the most powerful and distinctive sounds of eastern North American forests.

children.name: Mniotilta
children.description: The black-and-white warbler — a distinctive monotypic genus with a unique foraging behaviour that sets it apart from all other Parulidae. It creeps along tree trunks and branches like a nuthatch, probing bark crevices for hidden insects. Its black-and-white streaked plumage resembles that of a tiny woodpecker, and its squeaky, wheel-like song is a familiar sound of North American woodlands.

children.name: Parkesia
children.description: The waterthrushes — a small genus of large, terrestrial warblers restricted to wet habitats. They resemble thrushes in build and behaviour, with heavily streaked underparts and a habit of bobbing their rear body. They walk on the ground along streams and in swamps, flipping dead leaves in search of insects, and are among the most secretive of North American warblers despite their size.

children.name: Parkesia noveboracensis
children.description: The northern waterthrush (Parkesia noveboracensis) It is a rare vagrant to other South American countries and to western Europe.

children.name: Cardellina
children.description: A small genus of colourful warblers with predominantly red or yellow plumage, including the redstarts and the Canada Warbler. They are active, acrobatic foragers of montane and boreal forests across the Americas.

children.name: Cardellina canadensis
children.description: The Canada warbler (Cardellina canadensis) is a small boreal songbird of the New World warbler family (Parulidae).

children.name: Leiothlypis
children.description: A genus of small, plain-faced warblers with thin pointed bills and predominantly olive or grey upperparts. They forage deliberately in trees and shrubs, and are among the most common Neotropical migrants in North America.

children.name: Leiothlypis peregrina
children.description: The Tennessee warbler (Leiothlypis peregrina) is a New World warbler that breeds in eastern North America and winters in southern Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America.

children.name: Leiothlypis ruficapilla
children.description: The Nashville warbler (Leiothlypis ruficapilla) is a small songbird in the New World warbler family, found in North and Central America.

children.name: Leiothlypis crissalis
children.description: The Colima warbler (Leiothlypis crissalis) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Oporornis
children.description: A monotypic genus of secretive, skulking warbler with a preference for wet boreal forests and bogs. It is more often heard than seen, delivering its distinctive song from deep within dense spruce and tamarack stands.

children.name: Oporornis agilis
children.description: The Connecticut warbler (Oporornis agilis) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.

children.name: Vermivora
children.description: A small genus of brightly coloured warblers with bold wing patterns and relatively large bills. They are among the most sought-after warblers by birders due to their striking beauty and the conservation concern surrounding some species.

children.name: Myioborus
children.description: The whitestarts or redstarts — a genus of brightly coloured warblers with vivid red, yellow, and black plumage and distinctive white outer tail feathers that are constantly fanned. They are active, acrobatic foragers of montane forests from the southwestern United States through the Andes.

children.name: Myioborus pictus
children.description: The painted redstart or painted whitestart (Myioborus pictus) is a species of New World warbler found in mountainous areas across inland Central America.

children.name: Myioborus torquatus
children.description: The collared whitestart (Myioborus torquatus), also known as the collared redstart, is a tropical New World warbler endemic to the mountains of Costa Rica and western-central Panama.

children.name: Myioborus cardonai
children.description: The Guaiquinima whitestart (Myioborus cardonai), also known as the Guaiquinima redstart, saffron-breasted whitestart or saffron-breasted redstart, is a species of bird in the family Parulidae.

children.name: Myioborus pariae
children.description: The Paria whitestart (Myioborus pariae), also known as the Paria redstart, yellow-faced whitestart or yellow-faced redstart, is a passerine bird of the New World warbler family, Parulidae.

children.name: Basileuterus

children.name: Basileuterus tacarcunae

children.name: Basileuterus ignotus

children.name: Basileuterus cabanisi
children.description: Cabanis's Warbler has a grey head, white supercilium, olive upperparts, and yellow underparts, found in the Andes from Peru to Bolivia. It inhabits the understorey of montane forests, often joining mixed-species flocks.

children.name: Myiothlypis
children.description: A genus of small warblers formerly included in Basileuterus, distinguished by their ground-foraging habits and often duller plumage. They are widespread in Central and South America, inhabiting forest understorey and edges.

children.name: Myiothlypis mesoleuca

children.name: Limnothlypis

children.name: Euthlypis

Both sexes are a light greyish brown with dark brown centres to the feathers, which give the appearance of stripes.

Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests, subtropical or tropical mangrove forests, and subtropical or tropical moist montane forests.

children.name: Myzomela obscura
children.description: The dusky myzomela or dusky honeyeater (Myzomela obscura) is a small, brown bird that is a common resident of the Aru Islands, southern New Guinea and northern and eastern Australia, where there are two separated populations, one in the Top End, another from Cape York Peninsula along the east coast as far south as the New South Wales border, though the species is rare south of Rockhampton.

children.name: Myzomela prawiradilagae
children.description: The Alor myzomela (Myzomela prawiradilagae) is a species of bird in the family Meliphagidae, the honeyeaters.

children.name: Myzomela rosenbergii
children.description: The red-collared myzomela is a species of bird in the family Meliphagidae. It is found in New Guinea. The long-billed myzomela of Goodenough Island was formerly considered conspecific, but was split as a distinct species by the IOC in 2021.

children.name: Myzomela rubratra

children.name: Myzomela rubrobrunnea

children.name: Manorina melanocephala
children.description: The noisy miner is a bird in the honeyeater family, Meliphagidae, and is endemic to eastern and southeastern Australia. This miner is a grey bird, with a black head, orange-yellow beak and feet, a distinctive yellow patch behind the eye, and white tips on the tail feathers. The Tasmanian subspecies has a more intense yellow panel in the wing, and a broader white tip to the tail.

children.name: Manorina melanophrys

children.description: The eastern spinebill (Acanthorhynchus tenuirostris) is a species of honeyeater found in south-eastern Australia in forest and woodland areas, as well as gardens in urban areas of Canberra, Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide and Hobart.

children.name: Dasyornis
children.description: A genus of secretive, ground-dwelling passerines endemic to Australia, characterised by the prominent bristles around the base of the bill for which they are named. They are stout, long-tailed birds with strong legs and a furtive nature, inhabiting dense heath, sedgeland, and coastal scrub. Their loud, ringing calls are far easier to hear than the birds themselves are to see.

children.name: Dasyornis brachypterus
children.description: The eastern bristlebird (Dasyornis brachypterus) is a species of bird in the bristlebird family, Dasyornithidae.

children.name: Dasyornis longirostris
children.description: The western bristlebird (Dasyornis longirostris) is a species of bird in the family Dasyornithidae.

children.name: Dasyornis broadbenti
children.description: The rufous bristlebird (Dasyornis broadbenti) is one of three extant species of bristlebirds.

children.name: Pardalotus
children.description: A genus of tiny, brightly coloured Australian passerines known as pardalotes, with short tails, stout bills, and dazzling spotted and striped plumage patterns. They are among the smallest birds in Australia, yet their rhythmic, bell-like songs are remarkably carrying. They are largely arboreal, feeding on insects and lerps in the canopy of eucalypts.

children.name: Pardalotus punctatus
children.description: The spotted pardalote (Pardalotus punctatus) is a small passerine bird native to eastern and southern Australia, at elevations of up to .

children.name: Pardalotus striatus
children.description: The striated pardalote (Pardalotus striatus) is the least colourful and most common of the four pardalote species.

children.name: Acanthiza
children.description: The thornbills — a genus of small, active insectivores with fine, pointed bills and a habit of flicking their wings while foraging. They are the most species-rich genus in the family, occupying virtually every terrestrial habitat across Australasia. Their calls are typically high-pitched and insect-like, and their social structures range from monogamous pairs to complex cooperative groups.

children.name: Acanthiza pusilla
children.description: thumb|A brown thornbill The brown thornbill (Acanthiza pusilla) is a passerine bird usually found in eastern and south-eastern Australia, including Tasmania.

children.name: Acanthiza lineata
children.description: The striated thornbill (Acanthiza lineata) is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae.

children.name: Acanthiza ewingii
children.description: The Tasmanian Thornbill (Acanthiza ewingii) is a small bushland member of the Acanthizidae (Australian warbler) family, endemic to Tasmania and the Bass Strait Islands.

children.name: Acanthiza herringi
children.description: A small thornbill with bold white eyebrow, found in dry woodlands of southeastern Australia.

children.name: Acanthiza inornata
children.description: The western thornbill (Acanthiza inornata) is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae.

children.name: Acanthiza magna
children.description: A thornbill with yellow tail from eastern Australia.

children.name: Acanthiza kelseyi
children.description: A thornbill from southwestern Australia.

children.name: Acanthornis
children.description: A monotypic genus of scrubtit from Tasmanian rainforests.

children.name: Aphelocephala
children.description: Small grey-brown warblers with distinctive white faces, endemic to Australia.

children.name: Aphelocephala leucopsis
children.description: The southern whiteface (Aphelocephala leucopsis) is a small passerine found in arid regions across most of the southern half of the Australian continent, excluding Tasmania.

children.name: Aphelocephala nigricincta
children.description: The banded whiteface (Aphelocephala nigricincta) is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae.

children.name: Calamanthus
children.description: Small, ground-dwelling warblers with finely streaked plumage, endemic to Australia.

children.name: Calamanthus fuliginosus
children.description: The striated fieldwren (Calamanthus fuliginosus) is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae, endemic to Australia.

children.name: Calamanthus campestris
children.description: The rufous fieldwren (Calamanthus campestris) also known as the desert wren or sandplain wren is a species of insectivorous bird in the family Acanthizidae, endemic to Australia.

children.name: Cincloramphus
children.description: A genus of large, grassland-dwelling warblers found across Australasia and the Pacific. They are robust, streaky birds with strong legs, adapted for a terrestrial lifestyle in open habitats. Their songs are often loud and complex, delivered from exposed perches or in flight.

children.name: Cincloramphus cruralis
children.description: The brown songlark (Cincloramphus cruralis), also Australian songlark, is a small passerine bird found throughout much of Australia.

children.name: Cincloramphus timoriensis
children.description: The tawny grassbird (Cincloramphus timoriensis) is a large songbird that is a member of the family Locustellidae commonly found in grassland and reedbed habitats.

children.name: Cincloramphus mathewsi
children.description: The rufous songlark (Cincloramphus mathewsi) is a species in the family Locustellidae endemic to Australia.

children.name: Cincloramphus macrurus
children.description: The Papuan grassbird (Cincloramphus macrurus) is a species of typical grassbird in the family Locustellidae.

children.name: Gerygone
children.description: The gerygones — a genus of small, insectivorous warblers found from Southeast Asia through Australasia to the Pacific islands. They are active, acrobatic foragers with fine, pointed bills and often brightly coloured facial patterns. Many species are known for their distinctive, descending songs, which give them their common name 'flyeaters'.

children.name: Gerygone caledonica
children.description: A gerygone from New Caledonia.

children.name: Gerygone chrysocras
children.description: A small warbler with bright yellow underparts, found in New Guinea.

children.name: Gerygone chrysogaster
children.description: The yellow-bellied gerygone is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae. The Yellow-Bellied Gerygone is native to New Guinea, typically found in subtropical or tropical moist lowlands forest. Shown to have least concern about population with it being very common, but is currently decreasing in population throughout New Guinea.

children.name: Gerygone cinerea
children.description: The grey thornbill, ashy gerygone or mountain gerygone (Acanthiza cinerea) is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae.

children.name: Gerygone dorsalis
children.description: The rufous-sided gerygone is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae. It is found in the eastern Lesser Sunda Islands and Kai Islands.

children.name: Gerygone flavolateralis
children.description: The fan-tailed gerygone is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae. It is found in New Caledonia and Vanuatu. The Rennell gerygone of the Solomon Islands was formerly considered conspecific, but was split as a distinct species by the IOC in 2021.

children.name: Gerygone fusca
children.description: The western gerygone (Gerygone fusca) is a small, brownish-grey species of passerine bird, which is found in inland and south-west Australia.

children.name: Gerygone igata
children.description: The grey warbler (Gerygone igata), also known by its Māori name or outside New Zealand as the grey gerygone, is an insectivorous bird in the family Acanthizidae endemic to New Zealand.

children.name: Gerygone inornata
children.description: The plain gerygone is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae. It is found on the islands of Wetar and Timor. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist lowland forest and subtropical or tropical mangrove forest.

children.name: Gerygone lateralis
children.description: Gerygone lateralis (Gerygone) is a australasian warblers species found in Asia region.

children.name: Gerygone levigaster
children.description: The mangrove gerygone (Gerygone levigaster) is a species of bird in the Australian warbler family Acanthizidae.

children.name: Gerygone modesta
children.description: The Norfolk gerygone is a species of bird in the Australian warbler family Acanthizidae. It is endemic to Norfolk Island. This species was once lumped with the grey gerygone of New Zealand and the extinct Lord Howe gerygone as a single species.

children.name: Gerygone mouki
children.description: The brown gerygone (Gerygone mouki), previously known as the brown warbler, is a small passerine bird native to eastern coastal Australia.

children.name: Gerygone palpebrosa
children.description: The fairy gerygone (Gerygone palpebrosa), previously known as the fairy warbler, is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae native to New Guinea and Queensland.

children.name: Gerygone tenebrosa
children.description: The dusky gerygone (Gerygone tenebrosa) is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae.

children.name: Hylacola
children.description: Small secretive warblers with rufous rumps, endemic to southern Australia.

children.name: Hylacola cauta
children.description: The shy heathwren (Hylacola cauta) is a species of small bird in the family Acanthizidae, endemic to Australia.

children.name: Mohoua
children.description: Mohoua — a genus of australasian warblers in the family Acanthizidae.

children.name: Mohoua albicilla
children.description: The whitehead is a species of small passerine bird endemic to New Zealand. It is classified in the family Mohouidae. The male whitehead's upperparts, wings and tail are a pale brown in colour, while the head and underparts are white – in the case of the male an almost pure white in colour.

children.name: Mohoua ochrocephala
children.description: The yellowhead or mohua is a small insectivorous passerine bird endemic to the South Island of New Zealand. Once a common forest bird, its numbers declined drastically after the introduction of rats and stoats, and its IUCN conservation status is now near threatened.

children.name: Oreoscopus
children.description: A monotypic genus of fernwren from Queensland rainforests.

children.name: Origma
children.description: Small active warblers of rocky habitats in Australia and New Guinea.

children.name: Origma rufogularis
children.description: A small warbler with rufous throat, found in rocky hills of southern New Guinea.

children.name: Pachycare
children.description: A monotypic genus of goldenface from the montane forests of New Guinea.

children.name: Poodytes
children.description: A genus of small, secretive grass-dwelling warblers endemic to Australia and New Zealand. They are skulking birds of dense grassland and swamp vegetation, with short tails and strong legs adapted for a terrestrial lifestyle.

children.name: Poodytes gramineus
children.description: The little grassbird (Poodytes gramineus) is a species of Old World warbler in the family Locustellidae.

children.name: Pyrrholaemus
children.description: Small ground-dwelling warblers with red-brown throats, endemic to Australia.

children.name: Pyrrholaemus sagittatus
children.description: The speckled warbler (Pyrrholaemus sagittatus) is a species of bird in the family Acanthizidae.

children.name: Sericornis
children.description: The scrubwrens — a genus of secretive, primarily ground-dwelling warblers with a furtive, mouse-like behaviour, found in the densest parts of forests and heathlands. They have short, rounded wings and strong legs, and their plumage is typically a rich blend of browns, olive-greens, and rufous. Most species are restricted to Australia and New Guinea.

children.name: Sericornis humilis
children.description: The Tasmanian scrubwren or brown scrubwren (Sericornis humilis) is a bird species endemic to the temperate forests of Tasmania and nearby King Island.

children.name: Sericornis beccarii
children.description: The tropical scrubwren or Beccari's scrubwren (Sericornis beccarii) is a bird species.

children.name: Sericornis novaeguineae
children.description: A large scrubwren found in the montane forests of New Guinea.

children.name: Sericornis rufescens
children.description: The Vogelkop scrubwren (Aethomyias rufescens) is a bird species in the family Acanthizidae.

children.name: Smicrornis
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Weebill, which at 8–9 cm is one of the smallest birds in Australia. It is a compact, active insectivore with a short tail, a pale, slightly curved bill, and a persistent, loud call that seems far too big for such a tiny bird. It is common across much of the continent in dry forests and woodlands.

children.name: Pomatostomus
children.description: The Australasian babblers — a genus of medium-sized, strongly social passerines with stout, decurved bills and long, broad tails held cocked at an angle. They live in closely bonded family groups of up to twenty birds that cooperate to build large, domed stick nests, defend territories, and rear young. Their rich, chattering calls are a characteristic sound of the Australian bush.

children.name: Pomatostomus isidorei
children.description: The Papuan babbler (Garritornis isidorei), New Guinea babbler, or Isidore's rufous babbler, is a species of bird in the family Pomatostomidae.

children.name: Orthonyx
children.description: A genus of unusual, ground-dwelling passerines endemic to eastern Australia and New Guinea, with a peculiar rigid tail structure adapted for bracing against the ground. Their legs are exceptionally powerful, used to sweep aside leaf litter in a distinctive sideways motion as they forage for invertebrates. They are among the most primitive living songbirds.

children.name: Orthonyx temminckii
children.description: The Australian logrunner (Orthonyx temminckii) is a species of bird that is endemic to eastern Australia where it uses unique foraging techniques and adaptations to search for its food on the floors of temperate, subtropical, or tropical moist lowland forests in south-eastern Australia.

children.name: Cnemophilus
children.description: A genus of stout, medium-sized passerines endemic to the montane forests of New Guinea, superficially resembling birds-of-paradise but now placed in their own family. Males are brilliantly coloured in iridescent blues, purples, and yellows, while females are dull olive-brown. Their diet consists primarily of fruit, and they build domed nests in tree forks.

children.name: Cnemophilus macgregorii
children.description: The crested satinbird (Cnemophilus macgregorii), formerly known as the crested bird-of-paradise, is a species of bird in the satinbird family Cnemophilidae.

children.name: Loboparadisea
children.description: A monotypic genus of satinbird endemic to the mountains of New Guinea, with the male possessing a bizarre fleshy yellow wattle around the bill. The genus name meaning 'lobe-paradise bird' reflects its historical misclassification as a bird-of-paradise. It is a frugivore of the mid-montane forests.

children.name: Melanocharis
children.description: The typical berrypeckers — a genus of small, fruit-eating passerines endemic to New Guinea, with short tails and fine, slightly curved bills. Their plumage is sexually dimorphic: males are glossy blue-black or olive above, yellow or white below, while females are duller. They inhabit montane and submontane forests, where they feed primarily on small fruits and berries.

children.name: Melanocharis nigra
children.description: The black berrypecker (Melanocharis nigra) is a species of bird in the family Melanocharitidae.

children.name: Melanocharis arfakiana
children.description: The obscure berrypecker (Melanocharis arfakiana) is a small passerine bird from the berrypecker family Melanocharitidae.

children.name: Melanocharis striativentris
children.description: The streaked berrypecker (Melanocharis striativentris) is a species of bird in the family Melanocharitidae.

children.name: Rhamphocharis nocturnalis
children.description: The Nocturnal Berrypecker is a nocturnal species that roosts in dense forest canopies, foraging primarily at night for small fruits and insects. Their feathers are adapted to reduce heat loss during the cool nights.

children.name: Rhamphocharis
children.description: A small genus of berrypeckers with notably thick, deep bills adapted for crushing seeds and hard fruits, endemic to the mountain forests of New Guinea. They are medium-sized by melanocharitid standards, with spotted underparts that provide good camouflage in the forest gloom.

children.name: Toxorhamphus
children.description: Small, long-billed berrypeckers found in New Guinea, closely related to the true berrypeckers. They have relatively long, slender bills adapted for feeding on nectar and small fruits, filling an ecological niche similar to sunbirds.

children.name: Oedistoma
children.description: Tiny, long-billed birds from New Guinea, among the smallest members of the berrypecker family. They have fine, decurved bills adapted for feeding on nectar and small insects, and were once considered part of the flowerpecker family.

children.name: Oedistoma iliolophus
children.description: The spectacled longbill (Oedistoma iliolophus), also known as dwarf longbill, plumed longbill or dwarf honeyeater, is a species of bird in the family Melanocharitidae.

children.name: Oedistoma pygmaeum
children.description: The pygmy longbill or pygmy honeyeater (Oedistoma pygmaeum) is a species of bird in the family Melanocharitidae.

children.name: Oedistoma spectaculare
children.description: A tiny longbill with a distinctive white eye-ring (spectacles), olive-green upperparts, and yellowish underparts, found in the montane forests of New Guinea. It has a fine decurved bill used for feeding on nectar and small insects. It is an active, acrobatic forager, often hovering at flowers.

children.name: Paramythia
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Eastern Crested Berrypecker, a medium-sized, strikingly coloured passerine endemic to the montane forests of New Guinea. Its most distinctive feature is the tall, bushy crest that gives it a regal appearance. Males and females are similar in plumage, unlike the closely related Oreocharis, and feed primarily on soft fruits.

children.name: Oreocharis
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Tit Berrypecker, a tiny, active bird superficially resembling a tit or a white-eye, endemic to the mountains of New Guinea. It is the smallest member of the painted berrypecker family, with a short, fine bill and a tendency to forage acrobatically in the outer foliage. Its bright yellow breast makes it a striking sight in the moss forests.

children.name: Oreocharis arfaki
children.description: The tit berrypecker (Oreocharis arfaki) is a species of bird in the family Paramythiidae.

children.name: Callaeas
children.description: The kokakos — a genus of large, arboreal passerines endemic to New Zealand, with grey plumage and striking blue or blue-black wattles on the face. They are largely frugivorous, with a specialised gizzard that helps process tough forest fruits. Their haunting, organ-like duetting song carries through the forest and is considered among the most beautiful of any New Zealand bird.

children.name: Philesturnus
children.description: The saddlebacks — a genus of striking black-and-chestnut birds endemic to New Zealand, named for the saddle-like chestnut patch across the back. They are highly active insectivores that forage on tree trunks and branches, probing bark crevices with their stout bills. They have been extensively translocated to predator-free islands and sanctuaries as a conservation measure.

children.name: Notiomystis
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Stitchbird, a unique New Zealand passerine that was long thought to be a honeyeater but is now placed in its own family. It has a brush-tipped tongue for nectar feeding and shows remarkable sexual dimorphism, with the male having a striking black-and-yellow head pattern. It is highly social and often visits feeding stations in sanctuaries.

children.name: Psophodes
children.description: A genus of medium-sized, crested passerines endemic to Australia, characterised by stout, wedge-shaped bills and loud, distinctive vocalisations. They are divided into two groups: the whipbirds, with a characteristic whip-crack song, and the wedgebills, with a softer, bubbling call. They inhabit dense undergrowth, where they forage on the ground for insects and seeds.

children.name: Psophodes olivaceus
children.description: The eastern whipbird (Psophodes olivaceus) is an insectivorous passerine bird native to the east coast of Australia.

children.name: Psophodes nigrogularis
children.description: The western whipbird (Psophodes nigrogularis) is a passerine bird found in several scattered populations in Southwest Australia.

children.name: Psophodes occidentalis
children.description: The chiming wedgebill (Psophodes occidentalis), sometimes referred to as chiming whipbird, is a species of bird in the family Psophodidae.

children.name: Psophodes cristatus
children.description: The chirruping wedgebill (Psophodes cristatus) is a medium-sized member of the genus Psophodes, which consists or four to five songbirds endemic to Australia.

children.name: Androphobus
children.description: A monotypic genus of whipbird-like bird found only in the highland forests of New Guinea. It was once considered a babbler but is now placed in the Psophodidae. Very little is known about its ecology and behaviour.

children.name: Androphobus viridis
children.description: The Papuan whipbird (Androphobus viridis) is a little-known and unobtrusive species of bird in the family Psophodidae.

children.name: Cinclosoma
children.description: The quail-thrushes — a genus of medium-sized, ground-dwelling passerines with a quail-like build, fine dark scalloping on the upperparts, and a distinctive white eyebrow stripe. They inhabit arid and semi-arid woodlands and shrublands across Australia, where they run rapidly through the undergrowth like small quail. They are secretive, usually detected by their fine, high-pitched calls.

children.name: Cinclosoma albiventre
children.description: A quail-thrush with white belly, found in northern Australia.

children.name: Cinclosoma alisteri
children.description: The Nullarbor quail-thrush is a species of bird in the family Cinclosomatidae. It is the only Australian bird endemic to the Nullarbor Plain in southern Australia.

children.name: Cinclosoma castaneothorax
children.description: The chestnut-breasted quail-thrush is a small endemic Australian bird which is predominantly found within the semi-arid deserts of New South Wales and Queensland.

children.name: Ptilorrhoa
children.description: The jewel-babblers — a genus of brilliantly coloured, ground-dwelling passerines endemic to the rainforests of New Guinea. Their name is well earned: they are among the most vividly plumaged of all Australasian passerines, with combinations of deep blues, purples, chestnut, and white. They run and hop along the forest floor with a distinctive bobbing gait.

children.name: Batis
children.description: The batises — a genus of small, strikingly patterned African flycatchers with a distinctive habit of cocking their tails and flicking their wings. They have a bold black face mask and a white or yellow eye-ring, giving them an alert, inquisitive expression. Unlike the wattle-eyes, they lack fleshy wattles and have a more slender build adapted for active flycatching.

children.name: Batis capensis
children.description: The Cape batis (Batis capensis) is a small, stout insect-eating passerine bird in the wattle-eye family.

children.name: Batis christiani
children.description: A batis found in the lowland forests of Ghana.

children.name: Batis diops
children.description: The Rwenzori batis (Batis diops) is a bird native to the Albertine Rift montane forests, where it inhabits altitudes of .

children.name: Batis fraenata
children.description: A small pygmy batis found in East African savannas.

children.name: Batis ituriensis
children.description: The Ituri batis or Chapin's batis (Batis ituriensis) is a species of bird in the wattle-eye family, Platysteiridae which is found in the humid forests of eastern central Africa.

children.name: Batis minulla
children.description: thumb|Angolan Batis female The Angola batis (Batis minulla) is a species of bird in the family Platysteiridae.

children.name: Batis mixta
children.description: The forest batis or short-tailed batis (Batis mixta) is a species of bird in the wattle-eye family, Platysteiridae occurring in eastern Africa.

children.name: Batis molitor
children.description: The chinspot batis (Batis molitor) is a small songbird of the genus Batis in the family Platysteiridae which is a common and widespread species in the woodlands of southern Africa from the Eastern Cape north to 3°N in southern Kenya and Gabon.

children.name: Batis perkeo
children.description: The pygmy batis (Batis perkeo) is a very small insectivorous bird which finds its food foraging among leaves, it is a member of the wattle-eyes family, the Platysteiridae.

children.name: Batis reichenowi
children.description: The forest batis or short-tailed batis (Batis mixta) is a species of bird in the wattle-eye family, Platysteiridae occurring in eastern Africa.

children.name: Batis senegalensis
children.description: The Senegal batis (Batis senegalensis) is a species of small passerine bird in the wattle-eyes family, Platysteiridae.

children.name: Batis soror
children.description: The pale batis (Batis soror), also known as the Mozambique batis or East coast batis is a species of small bird in the wattle-eyes family, Platysteiridae.

children.name: Bias
children.description: Bias — a genus of wattle-eyes & batises in the family Platysteiridae.

children.name: Bias musicus
children.description: The black-and-white shrike-flycatcher, also known as the black-and-white flycatcher or vanga flycatcher, is a species of passerine bird found in Africa. It was placed with the wattle-eyes and batises in the family Platysteiridae but is now considered to be more closely related to the helmetshrikes and woodshrikes.

children.name: Lanioturdus
children.description: Lanioturdus — a genus of wattle-eyes & batises in the family Platysteiridae.

children.name: Lanioturdus torquatus
children.description: The white-tailed shrike is a small passerine bird from the family Platysteiridae. It is also known as the chatshrike or ground batis. It occurs only in western Angola and Namibia in thorn scrub.

children.name: Platysteira
children.description: The wattle-eyes — a genus of small, robust African passerines with prominent fleshy wattles above the eyes that give them their distinctive name. The wattles are often brightly coloured in males and are used in courtship displays. They are active, restless insectivores that hawk for prey in the forest understorey, often joining mixed-species flocks.

children.name: Platysteira tonsa
children.description: The white-spotted wattle-eye is a species of bird in the wattle-eye family Platysteiridae. It is found in Cameroon, Central African Republic, Republic of the Congo, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ivory Coast, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, and Nigeria. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests and subtropical or tropical moist montane forests.

children.name: Bocagia
children.description: Bocagia - a genus in the family Malaconotidae.

children.name: Bocagia minuta
children.description: The marsh tchagra or blackcap bush-shrike (Bocagia minuta) is a species of passerine bird placed in the monotypic genus Bocagia in the family Malaconotidae..

children.name: Chlorophoneus
children.description: The green-and-yellow bushshrikes — a genus of medium-sized, colourful bushshrikes with greenish upperparts and bright yellow or orange underparts. They are more arboreal and slender-billed than Malaconotus, feeding primarily on insects gleaned from foliage. Their songs are rich, melodious, and often repetitive.

children.name: Chlorophoneus abscessus
children.description: A bushshrike from Central Africa.

children.name: Chlorophoneus olivaceus
children.description: The olive bushshrike (Chlorophoneus olivaceus) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae..

children.name: Dryoscopus
children.description: The puffbacks — a genus of medium-sized bushshrikes named for the male's dramatic display in which the loose feathers of the lower back and rump are fluffed out into a striking white ball. They are active, restless foragers with strong, slightly hooked bills, found across sub-Saharan Africa in woodlands and savannas. They are vocal birds with harsh, repetitive calls.

children.name: Dryoscopus gambensis
children.description: The northern puffback (Dryoscopus gambensis) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae.

children.name: Dryoscopus senex
children.description: Dryoscopus senex (Pale-billed Puffback) is a bushshrikes species found in Africa region.

children.name: Laniarius
children.description: The boubous and gonoleks — a genus of colourful bushshrikes with strong, stout bills and a characteristic duetting behaviour in which pairs sing precisely coordinated antiphonals. They are among the most brightly coloured bushshrikes, often combining black, white, and brilliant crimson or yellow underparts. They are secretive but highly vocal, inhabiting dense thickets and riparian vegetation.

children.name: Laniarius aethiopicus
children.description: The Ethiopian boubou (Laniarius aethiopicus) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae..

children.name: Laniarius amboimensis
children.description: The Gabela bushshrike (Laniarius amboimensis) or Amboim bushshrike is a bird in the family Malaconotidae..

children.name: Laniarius amboinensis
children.description: A boubou from the highlands of East Africa.

children.name: Laniarius atroflavus
children.description: The yellow-breasted boubou (Laniarius atroflavus) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae..

children.name: Laniarius barbarus
children.description: The yellow-crowned gonolek (Laniarius barbarus), also known as the common gonolek, is a medium-sized passerine bird in the bushshrike family..

children.name: Laniarius barbatus
children.description: A boubou with yellow breast from Central Africa.

children.name: Laniarius bicolor
children.description: thumb|Perched in riparian vegetation, coastal Angola The swamp boubou (Laniarius bicolor), also known as the Gabon boubou, is a species of bird in the Malaconotidae or bushshrike family.

children.name: Laniarius brauni
children.description: Braun's bushshrike (Laniarius brauni) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae..

children.name: Laniarius erlangeri
children.description: The black boubou (Laniarius nigerrimus), also known as Somali boubou, Erlanger's boubou or coastal boubou, is a medium-size bushshrike.

children.name: Laniarius erythrogaster
children.description: The black-headed gonolek (Laniarius erythrogaster) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae..

children.name: Laniarius ferrugineus
children.description: thumb|right|Call of L.

children.name: Laniarius leucogaster
children.description: A boubou with white underparts from sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Laniarius major
children.description: The tropical boubou or bell shrike (Laniarius aethiopicus) is a medium-sized passerine bird of sub-Saharan Africa..

children.name: Laniarius mufumbiri
children.description: The papyrus gonolek (Laniarius mufumbiri) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae.

children.name: Laniarius nigerrimus
children.description: The black boubou (Laniarius nigerrimus), also known as Somali boubou, Erlanger's boubou or coastal boubou, is a medium-size bushshrike..

children.name: Laniarius rufispectus
children.description: Laniarius rufispectus (Rufous-breasted Boubou) is a bushshrikes species found in Africa region.

children.name: Laniarius somalicus
children.description: A boubou from the Horn of Africa.

children.name: Laniarius sublacteus
children.description: The East Coast boubou or Zanzibar boubou (Laniarius sublacteus) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae..

children.name: Malaconotus
children.description: The large bushshrikes — a genus of robust, heavy-billed African passerines with powerful hooked bills adapted for taking large prey including vertebrates. They are the largest bushshrikes, with a deliberate, slow-moving foraging style that belies their fierce predatory nature. Their calls are deep, mournful whistles that carry long distances through the forest.

children.name: Nilaus
children.description: Nilaus — a genus of bushshrikes in the family Malaconotidae.

children.name: Rhodophoneus
children.description: A monotypic genus of bushshrike containing the Rosy-patched Bushshrike, a striking inhabitant of arid scrublands in eastern Africa. It has a unique plumage pattern with a vivid crimson patch on the throat and breast, and is more terrestrial than other bushshrikes, often running on the ground.

children.name: Tchagra
children.description: The tchagras — a genus of medium-sized bushshrikes with a distinctive crown pattern featuring a black lateral stripe edged with white, giving them a capped appearance. They have relatively slender, hooked bills and long, graduated tails, and are more terrestrial than other bushshrikes. They inhabit scrub, savanna, and forest edge habitats across Africa.

children.name: Tchagra minuta
children.description: The marsh tchagra or blackcap bush-shrike (Bocagia minuta) is a species of passerine bird placed in the monotypic genus Bocagia in the family Malaconotidae.

children.name: Tchagra senegalus
children.description: The black-crowned tchagra (Tchagra senegalus) is a bushshrike..

children.name: Telophorus
children.description: A genus of beautiful, colourful bushshrikes with green upperparts and brightly coloured underparts in shades of orange, red, or yellow. They are forest and woodland dwellers that forage actively in the canopy, gleaning insects from leaves. Their songs are rich, musical, and often delivered in duet.

children.name: Telophorus cruentus
children.description: The rosy-patched bushshrike (Rhodophoneus cruentus) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae..

children.name: Telophorus olivaceus
children.description: The olive bushshrike (Chlorophoneus olivaceus) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae.

children.name: Telophorus viridis
children.description: The gorgeous bushshrike (Telophorus viridis) is a species of bird in the family Malaconotidae.

children.name: Machaerirhynchus
children.description: A genus of small, broad-billed passerines endemic to New Guinea and northeastern Queensland, named for their unusually wide, flat bills that are shaped like a boat.
